The access model decides what people can have, how they get it, and who says yes. On this program it grew to about 3,300 access profiles and 280 roles, almost all of them generated or bulk-created. This page covers the building blocks, the four ways access reached users, and the decisions about approval, ownership and revocation that are easy to leave at the defaults.

Object | What it is | How we used it |
Entitlement | One permission on a source (group, role, assignment) | Aggregated from the source. Mostly not requestable directly |
Access profile | A bundle of entitlements from one source, with an approval scheme | The unit users request. Nearly always one entitlement each |
Role | A bundle of access profiles, assigned by criteria or requested | Criteria-based birthright roles; one requestable role |
Source app | The Request Center / App Center tile for a source | Groups access profiles so users can browse them |
Launcher + workflow + form | A custom request experience | For access that cannot be modelled as a profile |
Governance group | A set of people who act as reviewers or approvers | Reviewers for campaigns, second-level approvers |

chunks.h: Four ways access reaches a user
chunks.x:
Access profile in the Request Center. The standard path. A profile wraps an entitlement, carries the approval scheme and belongs to a source app (the tile). If a profile belongs to no app it is still requestable by search but has no tile.
Launcher plus workflow. A form-driven request that ends in a workflow granting access directly. Used when selections are composite (client, group, office) and need dynamic option lists.
Criteria-based role. Membership defined by identity attributes; assignment is automatic and silent. Used for per-location baseline groups and for entitlements that follow someone's directory presence.
Aggregation only. The source is read and reviewed, nothing is granted from ISC. Many sources, and one live integration, sat here.
Which mechanism you choose per application is a design decision with consequences:
Mechanism | Pros | Cons |
Profile + tile | Familiar, supports approval chains, browsable | Becomes unbrowsable at scale. One integration had 1,700 profiles and no tile: users had to search by name, following a naming convention |

chunks.h: Four ways access reaches a user
chunks.x:
Launcher + workflow | Dynamic forms, composite grants | Platform limits on forms and workflows (next page). Only works if every grant goes through the launcher |
Criteria role | No request needed | No record explains why someone gained or lost it; membership flips on identity refresh |
Aggregation only | Cheap, immediate review | No provisioning; revocation may be the only write |

About 280 roles existed, 282 of them criteria-based and none of them requestable but one. The overwhelming pattern was a birthright role per office, each wrapping an access profile of the AD groups that office needs. This is how the location-to-default-groups mapping from the legacy tool was reproduced.
Notes:
Name them predictably (<Office>_BirthRight). A second family of per-country roles existed for another group set.
Some roles held no access profile. They were placeholders created in bulk. Empty roles are noise in every campaign and report; either fill or remove them.
Role criteria are evaluated on refresh. A change in location or lifecycle state changes membership, which provisions or removes access, with no request. Document that in your SOP so service desks know the access came from a role.
Role propagation was disabled in the tenant. Know the setting; it governs whether role changes cascade as expected.
Criteria built on the lifecycle state attribute (active, or not inactive) keep leavers from retaining visibility of request forms.

Topic | What we saw |
Count | About 3,300, of which about 3,100 requestable |
Naming | <App> - <Scope>: <Role> for generated ones; the description mirrored the name. A search by name is the discovery route for untiled profiles |
Entitlement coverage | 2,071 entitlements produced 1,738 profiles on one source, so about 330 were governed but not requestable. Decide whether that is intentional |
Ownership | One person owned 2,700 of the 3,000 profiles we sampled. Every profile change, certification review and escalation routed through them. Use a governance group |
Revocation approval | Mostly none. About 20 percent of profiles in the sample had a manager approval on revocation. See below |
Denial comments | Required on one application, not on the rest. Pick a policy |
Duration and re-authorisation | No profile set a maximum duration or a required end date. Re-authorisation was off tenant-wide |
Approval schemes seen

Scheme | Used for |
Manager only | The default for most applications |
Manager then a governance group | High-risk applications such as the finance consolidation tool; the second stage is an application owner group |
Owner only | A handful |
None (empty list) | A lift-and-shift application where the ITSM ticket already had approval |
Revocation approval is a decision
On most profiles granting required manager approval and revoking required nothing. That asymmetry is often right (removing access should be easy) but it must be chosen, documented and defended. It also means anyone with a way to raise a revoke can remove access with no check. Record the decision per application.
Tenant-wide request settings
These settings were read from the tenant and are worth reviewing on day one:
Request on behalf of: anyone could request for anyone. Tighten if your policy requires managers or owners only.
Auto-approval: off.

Reauthorisation: off.
Approval reminders and escalation: no days, no maximum, no fallback approver. Approvals can sit forever, and the "approval expired" case in a workflow looks identical to "never arrived" (see the forms page). Set reminders and a fallback.
Entitlement requests: allowed, comments optional.
Governance group visibility: off.

A source app's profile list is only visible through its own sub-resource. The list payload returned an empty accessProfiles array for apps that clearly had profiles. And that sub-resource returns an empty list silently when limit exceeds 250. Always page at 250.
One application had its profiles split across several tiles by scope (local, market, region, global). Splitting by scope made 200 profiles browsable. It cost four apps to maintain.
When access exists that has no profile (for example security groups held by a colleague that you are asked to replicate), a new "other" tile was created for the leftovers. Plan for an "everything else" tile instead of building profiles on demand.

Make entitlements non-requestable by default and expose access only through profiles. Exceptions bypass approval schemes. One integration had a single directly requestable entitlement that bypassed two-stage approval; find these with a search and close them.
If the entitlement catalogue is huge and mostly unneeded for requests (tens of thousands of role assignments), do not wrap them all in profiles. Review them; request only what is asked for.

Tags on entitlements (about 4,000 tagged) were used to scope reviews and searches, for example one tag per client entity. Tags are queryable in search and in form data sources, and they can replace what attributes cannot do (see the forms page).
Governance metadata attributes (privacy, classification, risk, environment, requires training and similar) exist in the platform. They were present but barely used. If audit wants classification on access, populate them at onboarding, not later.

Two interfaces for one app is a UX failure. A joiner form plus the Request Center produced two ways to request access for a single product. Choose one entry point per application.
Visibility of the launcher is itself an entitlement. See the forms page. A criteria role can control who sees the tile.
Third-party identities. If any applications serve clients, keep them out of the request center for employees.
Search-based discovery. Where an application has no tile, give users the naming convention, not a hope.

45 groups, mostly "<Application> Access Reviewers" of one to four people. They double as campaign reviewers and second-stage approvers.
Create them before campaigns and before approval schemes reference them. The rollout checklist had a dedicated task for source and approval groups.
Groups of one are an outage waiting for a holiday. Aim for at least two people per group.

Choose the access mechanism per application and record the reason.
Make entitlements non-requestable and wrap them in profiles.
Move profile ownership to governance groups before the count passes a few hundred.
Decide approval and revocation policy per application, with reminders and a fallback approver.
Define what happens to untiled access (an "others" app or an explicit no).

chunks.x:
SailPoint ISC Greenfield Implementation Field Guide
On this page
What the estate looked like

Rules the platform enforces
The campaign factory

Failure modes seen
What SailPoint's documentation adds

Access reviews were the part of the program with the most volume and the least product support. By the end the tenant held about 500 campaigns built from about 520 templates, and most of them were quarterly reviews of applications that had no live connector. This page covers how the review estate got that big, the decisions that shaped it, and the script that made it manageable.

Item | Scale |
Campaigns | about 500: roughly 440 search-based, about 60 source-owner |
Status | about 400 completed, about 100 active |
Templates | about 520 |
Governance groups used as reviewers | 45, each of one to four people, named "<Application> Access Reviewers" |
Auto-approval / reauthorisation | both off |
Flat-file sources | about 120, most of them feeding reviews |
Two things stand out. First, most reviews ran on flat files. For an application with no connector, the cheapest way to get its access into ISC is a CSV of user and entitlement, loaded through a delimited-file or SQL-loader source, then reviewed like any other source. Second, some of those sources were named per reviewer and per quarter. That looks like a source created for each review cycle (an inference from the names, so check your own tenant), which is why the source count reached the hundreds.

The application cannot be integrated yet, but audit wants evidence of a periodic review now.
The application is integrated read-only in a later phase, and the review is the bridge.
The access list comes from a report the application owner already produces.
The trade-off is that a flat-file review is only as good as the file. Nothing keeps it fresh, nothing reconciles it to the real application, and the correlation to identities depends on a single column. Treat it as a review input, not as a system of record.

Type | Reviews | Use it for |
Search-based (access) | Entitlements held by correlated accounts, selected by a search query | Almost everything. Scope with a query on source, tag or metadata |
Source owner | All accounts on a source, including uncorrelated ones | Accounts that did not match an identity. The source owner is the only person who can judge them |
Identity | Everything a person holds | Manager reviews of a team. Heavy on reviewers |
Uncorrelated accounts never appear in an access campaign. If you do not run a source-owner campaign too, they are never reviewed, and they tend to be the riskiest accounts on the source.

Reviewers cannot review their own access. ISC moves the item to the reviewer's manager. Expect "unexpected reviewer" noise and tell reviewers why.
A campaign that selects nothing is created empty. It does not error. Either the accounts are uncorrelated or nobody holds the access.
Reviewer names must be unique. A display name that matches two people fails. Use an email address.
Reminders, escalation and reassignment are organisation-level settings, not per campaign. Set them before the first launch.
A campaign decision does not always remove access. Revocation in a flat-file source only creates a task or a ticket. Say so in the reviewer instructions.

Creating hundreds of campaigns by hand is not credible, and the mistakes (wrong source, wrong reviewer, a stale file) are only found after launch. We built a Python tool, driven by a workbook, to create them safely. The design is worth copying whatever language you use.
Factory design. Dry run, snapshot and restore, staged creation and verification are the safety properties worth copying in any language.
The workbook
Sheet | Holds |
Settings | Tenant, API client, file server, behaviour switches |
Sources | One row per source: name, file, which column is the id, which is the correlation attribute, which columns are entitlements |
Campaigns | One row per campaign: source, scope, reviewer or governance group, deadline, type |
Column header prefixes tell the tool what a column is, and they combine: I_ identifier, D_ display name, E_ entitlement, C_ correlation attribute. A column called I_D_UserName is both the id and the display name.

What a run does
Preflight. The workbook can be saved, the API login works, the file server login works, settings are valid. If any of this fails, nothing has changed.
Plan. Every source and every campaign row is validated: reviewer found, group exists, entitlement column present. A bad source is skipped and recorded, the rest go on.
Run, per source. Snapshot the source settings, schema and correlation. Upload a clean copy of the file. Update the source settings. Aggregate. Remove stale accounts. Create the campaigns.
Safety properties
Property | How |
Never launches | Campaigns are created STAGED. Any call that activates, completes or reassigns a campaign is refused inside the script |
Dry run | --dry-run reads and validates everything and changes nothing |
Partial runs | --only A3,ADP limits the run to named sources |
Resume | --retry-failed repeats only what failed, and rows already marked complete are skipped |

Idempotent | An identical file already on the server is reused. Settings already in place are left alone |
No silent overwrite | A different file with the same name is never replaced: the new one is uploaded with a _qar suffix |
Undo | Every source's settings, schema and correlation are snapshotted. --restore latest puts them back after a typed confirmation |
Explains itself | Every failure is reported as WHY it happened, DO what to do, and the STATE it left behind |
Exit code | 1 when anything was discrepant, so it can sit in a pipeline |
Choices that mattered
Correlation column by match rate. Rather than trusting the file's author, the tool tests the candidate columns (email, login name) against the identity cube and picks the one that matches most accounts.
Stale account removal with a guard. Accounts in ISC but not in the new file are removed, unless that would exceed a configured percentage. This stops a truncated file from emptying a source.

Wait for the identity refresh. After removing stale accounts, the tool waits before creating the campaign, otherwise the removed accounts are still in the review.
Reviewer fallback. A blank reviewer means the user's manager. A governance group can be named instead.
Add new attributes before removing old ones. ISC will not delete or rename an attribute that a correlation rule, identity profile or entitlement uses ("Object in use by another"). Adding first and removing last avoids the deadlock.

The most valuable addition came later: after each campaign is created, still STAGED, compare it to the file it was built from.
Download ISC's own Campaign Status Report CSV for the campaign. If it cannot be produced, read the same facts from the review items through the API.
Read the flat file back from the file server, the one the source really loads, not the local copy.
Compare, for the campaign's own scope only.
Three numbers per campaign are put side by side: what the file holds, what should be in the campaign, and what is in it.
Row | Meaning |
users | distinct people holding at least one in-scope entitlement |
distinct entitlements | different entitlement values |
user + entitlement pairs | what a reviewer has to decide on |
per-user min / avg / max | how many each person holds |
"Should be in the campaign" is the file minus what ISC cannot include: uncorrelated accounts for an access campaign, and the inverse for a source-owner campaign.

Result | Meaning |
OK | Every expected pair is in the campaign and nothing else |
Missing from campaign | The file has it and the account is correlated, but the campaign lacks it. The load missed it, or the search index was behind, or there is no reviewer |
Extra in campaign | A stale account, or a value no longer in the file |
Uncorrelated user in access campaign | An uncorrelated account leaked into a campaign meant for correlated people |
Unexpected reviewer (a note, not a failure) | ISC moved a self-review to the manager |
The evidence is kept: a per-campaign report, a discrepancy list with likely reasons and the original status CSV from ISC.
Limits of the check
People are matched by display name. Two people with the same name collapse into one, which can hide an offsetting error.
Entitlement values are matched ignoring case but counted exactly. ISC shows Lda and LDA as one value.
User ids that differ only in case (USER01 and user01 in the same file) make ISC drop the rows of one spelling. The tool unifies them when it writes the file and reports any that were already loaded wrongly.

ISC's CSV adds a leading apostrophe to values that start with -. The check removes it.
Identity campaigns are not compared pair by pair.
A campaign checked after launch is still compared, but decisions already made do not change the item list.

chunks.h: Scoping reviews with tags and metadata
chunks.x: Tags on entitlements (about 4,000 were tagged) and a governance metadata attribute marking the review population let search-based campaigns select exactly the entitlements in scope. One tag per client entity, for example, produces one campaign per entity without touching the template. A tag-based scope also survives new entitlements being aggregated, where a hand-picked list does not.

Symptom | Cause | Fix |
Campaign created, zero reviews | Accounts uncorrelated, or nobody holds that access | Source-owner campaign, or fix correlation |
Reviewer not found | Display name matched two people | Use email |
Reviewer group not found | No governance group of that exact name | Create the group first; the error lists close names |
Entitlement not found | The value is not in the loaded file | Check spelling, or select every entitlement |
Aggregation did not finish | The load failed | Check source health and the connection, retry |
A same-named file already on the server | Someone else's file | Upload as _qar, then reconcile by hand |
Workbook will not save | Open in Excel | Close it |

Reassignment (reassigning certifications): the reviewer gives a reason in the comments, ISC checks the person being certified will not end up reviewing their own access, and automated reassignment stops after four hops, leaving the item with the fifth person in the chain. Long chains of "not mine" therefore end up on someone by accident.
No automatic reviewer failover after launch, according to community answers. Set up work reassignment for planned absences before the campaign starts.
Reminders go to reviewers weekly until they finish unless reminder emails are disabled. Escalation behaviour for IdentityIQ is described at length in the community; confirm the ISC equivalent before promising reviewers one.
Delimited files must be sorted by account ID, or a campaign can show one entitlement per account (see the connectors page). The factory's file writer should sort on the id column. Files over 500 MB are outside the documented comfort zone.

API pacing. A factory that creates hundreds of campaigns shares the 100 requests per 10 seconds allowance per client ID and API version. Add backoff on 429 using the Retry-After header, and give the tool its own API client.
A custom escalation workflow from the community handles 250 items at a time, which mirrors the parallel loop cap. If you build one, use a serial loop for larger sets.

Decide per application whether it is reviewed on a live connector or a flat file, and record why.
Create governance groups before campaigns reference them, with at least two people each.
Automate campaign creation, always create STAGED, and add a dry run and a snapshot-and-restore from day one.
Verify every campaign against its source file before launch. Keep the evidence.
Run a source-owner campaign for uncorrelated accounts, or accept in writing that they go unreviewed.
Set reminders, escalation and reassignment at the organisation level before the first launch.
Tell reviewers what a revoke decision will and will not do on a flat-file source.

Active Directory was the first target and the one every user notices. It was also the place where the legacy tool's behaviour had to be reproduced most faithfully, because changing naming, container placement or group membership rules affects mail, VPN, single sign-on and licensing at once.

Source | Purpose |
Main corporate domain | The primary workforce directory; create, move, enable, disable, group membership |
Administrator accounts in the same domain | Privileged accounts with their own correlation rule |
Second corporate domain | A separate domain with its own joiner and rehire workflows |
External-user domain | A third domain for external staff; it shared an Asia-region cluster with the second domain |
A product governed through AD groups | A fund-accounting product whose access is AD group membership, so it is an AD source in its own right |
Use one AD source per domain, one cluster per estate. Do not stretch one source across forests.

The create policy for the main domain defined about 50 fields. The important ones:
Field | How it is set |
sAMAccountName | A cloud rule: first 3 of first name + last 3 of last name + a two-digit counter, 8 characters maximum, with a uniqueness check |
cn | The login name, which keeps the distinguished name unique across containers |
distinguishedName | CN=<cn>, plus a path built from region, department and work location. Built by a transform on the identity |
mail, userPrincipalName, proxyAddresses | A cloud rule generates a unique address; UPN equals mail; proxy addresses hold the primary SMTP and the SIP address |
manager | A transform that finds the manager's distinguished name |
displayName, title, department, company, co, c, l, physicalDeliveryOfficeName, employeeType | Direct identity attribute mappings |
employeeID | The HR identifier |
extensionAttribute1, extensionAttribute2, a custom department attribute | Used by sync into the cloud directory and by downstream apps |

info | A note "Created by SailPoint Automation on <date>" |
pwdLastSet | Forces a change at first sign-in |
password | See the warning below |
The disable policy moves the object to a disabled container, hides it from the address list and stamps a note. The enable policy moves it back, un-hides it, sets a new password and stamps a note.
Do not derive passwords from HR attributes. The policy built the initial password by concatenating slices of HR attributes. That is deterministic and guessable by anyone who knows the pattern and has the HR record. Use a generated random value or a temporary access pass, deliver it through a controlled channel (to the manager only), and force a change on first sign-in.
Account build. Adapted from the joiner flow in the design: the same rules produce the login, email, location in the tree and baseline access.

Container (OU) placement depends on location. The legacy tool had large spreadsheets mapping office location to default groups, country finance and HR contacts, and web-presence contacts. Port the contacts into lookup transforms. Port the default groups into criteria-based birthright roles, one per office, each wrapping an access profile of that office's groups (see the access model page). Keep the source spreadsheet under change control.
Default groups per location are part of onboarding. In hypercare the first thing missed for one office was its default security groups for the internet gateway and remote access; without them users could not browse or connect from home. Verify each office's default group set during UAT, not only the global ones.
Baseline groups for every joiner: cloud sync, multi-factor authentication, self-service password reset, an "all IDM users" group, and a licence group. A different licence group applies to one country, so the licence logic is conditional on country.

Groups to preserve on leaver. Domain users plus the cloud-sync group must survive for a week or more after termination so mail and records stay reachable. Implement as an allow-list.
Group aggregation timing. If you read groups into ISC, aggregate them before accounts. Newly created accounts otherwise reference group objects ISC has not seen.
Standard human-account scope
Directory aggregation should read only the OUs that hold human accounts. A reconciliation file listing the standard human OUs (and the accounts under them) was used to confirm scope. Service accounts and shared mailboxes in those OUs end up uncorrelated or, worse, disabled by lifecycle actions. Decide:
Which OUs are in scope for aggregation.
How non-human accounts are identified (naming, an attribute, an OU).
Whether they get a separate source and profile.

A before-provisioning cloud rule on the main domain handled everything the policy could not. Its 16 KB of Java covered:
Name-change movers. Generate a new unique address (first.last, then first.last1...), set mail and UPN, rebuild proxy addresses with the new primary and the old one demoted, and optionally rename the object when the OU changes at the same time.
Leaver group cleanup. Remove every group except an allow-list.
Distinguished name targets read from identity attributes.
Guidance for this kind of rule:
Keep it as small as you can. It is a sandboxed Beanshell script; you cannot unit test it outside the platform and every change is a production change.
Log inputs and decisions at a low level and turn logging off after a diagnostic window. The rule logged mover details at error level, which buried genuine errors.
Handle the both changed at once case (name and OU in the same refresh) explicitly. It is easy to forget and it happens.

A stock "services standard" before-provisioning rule also sat in the tenant. Know whether you use it; do not delete it without checking references.
Directory agents. The design ran two agent servers per domain behind a load balancer, so an agent can be patched or fail without stopping provisioning. Reads go directly from the appliance; writes go through the agent.

chunks.h: Native rules on the directory source
chunks.x: An AfterModify native rule ran on the main domain source. IQService can run before and after scripts around operations. Use them sparingly: they run on the Windows host, outside the cloud rule sandbox, and they are the place where mailbox and licence side effects live if you keep them as scripts.

The legacy IDM ran PowerShell for several cloud mail operations. Decide where each lands:
Legacy step | Options in the new design |
Add baseline and licence groups on create | Directory group membership in the create policy, or an IQService after-script |
Convert to shared mailbox on leave | A script, or a group-based policy on the mail side |
Set out-of-office with the manager's text | A script run from a workflow or an after-script, using the leaver form answer |
Hide from the address list | A directory attribute set in the disable policy (what we used) |
Assign a leaver licence | A licence group added on disable |
Log which licence was assigned | An audit trail somewhere; the legacy scripts wrote files |
Authentication for mail scripts moved from basic authentication to certificate-based authentication during the legacy period. Do not build new automation on basic authentication.

The main domain aggregated every two hours across the night and day; the HR source every hour. Offset the two so a joiner's HR record, the directory create, the mail round-trip and the next directory aggregation line up.
Allow about an hour for a directory change to replicate across domain controllers before assuming a failure.
Set the delete threshold to 10% on every directory source. A bad LDAP search or a lost domain controller can return nothing.

Symptom | Cause |
Account missing in AD although a "credentials sent" email went out | Duplicate distinguished name or non-unique UPN rejected the create; fix the data, then re-provision from ISC |
User name shows as login ID in the admin console | CN equals login name by design |
Display name has two spaces | CN-derived name with no middle name; use a collapse-spaces transform |
Group membership gone after leaver date | No allow-list or no delay; see the lifecycle page |
Wrong HR or finance contact on a joiner | The contact lookup table is stale |
Rehire has the wrong mailbox state | The old mailbox was converted to shared; reactivation needs the reverse |
User cannot get online or on VPN | The location's default groups are missing |
Old and new accounts for the same person | The rehire rule was not followed in HR |

Port legacy contact mappings into lookup transforms with defaults and location-to-group mappings into per-office birthright roles.
Define the human-account OU scope and how you recognise non-human accounts.
Write the group allow-list for leavers and the delay.
Replace derived initial passwords with generated ones.
Decide the new home for every mailbox and licence script.
Set TLS and delete-threshold values on every directory source.

The last page is for the person on call. It lists the read-only API calls that explain most situations, then a symptom table generalised from the runbooks of several integrations. Everything here is safe to try first; none of the calls change anything unless marked.

Use a token with read scope. Version prefixes (v2025, beta) change over time, so confirm them against the current API reference.
text
```
GET  /v2025/sources/{id}
GET  /v2025/sources/{id}/schemas
GET  /v2025/sources/{id}/provisioning-policies
GET  /beta/sources/{id}/schedules
GET  /v2025/connector-rules
GET  /v2025/connector-rules/{id}
GET  /v2025/entitlements?filters=source.id eq "{id}"
GET  /v2025/access-profiles?limit=250
GET  /beta/source-apps
GET  /beta/source-apps/{id}/access-profiles?limit=250
GET  /v2025/roles
GET  /v2025/workflows
GET  /v2025/workflows/{id}
GET  /v2025/form-definitions
GET  /v2025/form-definitions/{id}
GET  /v2025/launchers
GET  /v2025/identity-profiles
POST /v2025/search
```
Call | Use it to | Watch out for |
Source, schemas, provisioning policies | See what a source is configured to do | A source can be configured to do nothing while rules do the work |
Schedules | Find sources with no aggregation schedule | An empty list is the finding |

Connector rules, by id | Read the script | Returns the script in clear text, including any embedded credential. Do not paste the output anywhere |
Entitlements filtered by source | Count and inspect | Counts that halve between runs mean a truncated load |
Access profiles | Inventory | Page at 250 |
Source apps and their sub-resource | See which profiles a tile holds | The list payload shows empty arrays. Use the sub-resource, and a limit above 250 returns an empty list silently |
Roles | Inventory criteria roles | Read the criteria; membership is attribute-driven |
Workflows and form definitions | Inspect triggers and steps | Secrets may be present. A launcher-driven form instance shows formData only in the list call |
Launchers | See what is exposed to users | Not patchable |
Identity profiles | Check mappings | Compare sandbox and production |
Search (POST) | Aggregations for counts, status and freshness | The best monitoring tool in the platform |

Two calls that change things
POST /v2025/accounts runs the connector's create operation and its before-rules. Use it to prove a create works. Use a test identity.
Configuration export with type RULE is the way to read cloud rules, which cannot be fetched with GET. Treat the export as sensitive.
Search recipes
Run these through the search API against the identities, accounts and entitlements indices. The query strings are ideas, not tested syntax: confirm the field names on your tenant first.
Question | Query idea |
Which sources have not aggregated recently? | Aggregation on the last aggregation date attribute, sorted ascending |
How many disabled accounts on a source? | Accounts query: source.name:"X" AND disabled:true, count only |
Who is uncorrelated? | Accounts query: uncorrelated:true on the source |
Which entitlements are directly requestable? | Entitlements query on requestable:true and compare with the intended set |

Did a literal placeholder leak? | An accounts or entitlements query for the placeholder string a rule is supposed to replace |
Who joined or left last night? | Identities query on created date or lifecycle state, with the attributes you want in the export |

Generalised from the runbooks of one REST integration, one JDBC integration with two instances and one REST integration for a finance system. Each row says what to suspect first, not the only possibility.
Aggregation and data
Symptom | Most likely cause | Check |
Aggregation fails right at the start | Token endpoint unreachable, or the client credentials were rotated | Test the token call from the appliance's network |
Aggregation "succeeds" but accounts carry error text | The error-detection settings in the source were altered, or the application changed its error wording | Compare the error strings with the source configuration |

Force a re-correlation
Accounts that stay uncorrelated after you fix a correlation rule or the data it matches were probably skipped by an optimized aggregation, which does not re-run correlation for unchanged accounts. Pace your scripts
The default allowance is 100 requests per client ID and API version per 10 seconds. A 429 response carries Retry-After. Sleep for that many seconds, then retry. Give automation its own API client.

Connecting an application is a pipeline of decisions, not a single configuration. This page covers how to choose a pattern, what to establish with the application team before you build, and what each integration style looked like in practice. The next page goes deep on the Web Services and JDBC connectors.

Apply these in order and stop at the first that fits.
Does the application authenticate through Active Directory? Govern the AD groups with the AD connector. You get provisioning, aggregation and certification of the access for free, and joiner and leaver already work because the directory does.
Is there a purpose-built connector? Use it (for example Dynamics 365, an ITSM product, a SaaS HR system). Check what it cannot do before you commit.
Is there a documented REST API for user and role management? Use Web Services. Expect to write rules.
Is there a database you may read, and a stored procedure or table you may write? Use JDBC. Expect to write a build-map rule and a provisioning rule.
None of the above? Load a flat file over SFTP. It supports aggregation, correlation and certification. Provisioning stays manual or ticket-based.
Nothing at all? Out of scope until the application changes.
Selection principle. Directory first, then a purpose-built connector, then web services or JDBC, then a flat file. A flat file is not a failure; it gave review coverage to most of the estate.

Two corollaries:
A flat file is not a failure. It gave review coverage to a large part of the application estate with near-zero build effort and no change to the application.
A ticket-based "disconnected" application is the last resort. If you must keep one, keep the ITSM ticket as the audit trail and plan to replace it.

Product names are used for commercial products; internal systems are described by pattern.
Active-Directory-governed product (fund accounting)
Access is membership of a handful of AD groups per instance. The product also requires a user to exist in the application before they can be granted access, and the reverse. Lesson: when an application is governed through AD, the integration is mostly access-model design.
Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations (native connector)
Users are synced from the cloud directory. The connector supported read, enable and disable, but not create, move, delete or group membership. The requirement document recorded that gap and that "client access is not in scope". Entitlements outnumbered users many times over (tens of thousands of organisation roles for a few thousand users), so aggregation volume and campaign size need planning. Workflow / BPM product with a REST API (Enate)
Three entitlement types: a user group (optional, specific to region and service line), and two mandatory roles. Access depends on the account existing in the product and matching the directory email. The second: a user chooses security groups according to function scope, so the access model needed a mapping between function and group.

Internal client-management portal (REST, POST only)
Two disjoint user populations behind one list endpoint, paging by page size with no overflow signal, tokens that expire with an HTTP 200 body, and revocation done entirely in rules that parse identifiers out of the entitlement name. Read access was solid; granting was absent in production.

HR / payroll SaaS products with simple APIs
Group aggregation did not exist (the product had no groups), so a "dummy" entitlement was created by an after-rule so access requests had something to attach to. Every one of the six custom integrations used the same trick: a rule sets IIQDisabled: true on the account map when the source says the account is inactive. No source mapped a native flag straight to the disabled state. Three consequences:
The decision is a string or boolean comparison in code. If the target changes its wording (InActive to Inactive), the comparison silently stops matching.
Rules that only ever set true rely on absence meaning enabled. Set both directions explicitly.
A token failure inside an after-rule that calls a second endpoint for the disabled list leaves everyone enabled. Log it and alert on it.

Checked against the account loading documentation and community threads on thresholds, October 2026.
The account delete threshold, precisely
The setting is the maximum percentage of accounts that can be deleted in one aggregation. Over the limit, the documentation says the aggregation is cancelled and a warning generated. A related multi-host page says deletions are skipped instead, so confirm which you get on your source type by testing, and monitor for the warning either way.
It must be an integer from 1 to 100. The UI dropdown reportedly lists values only up to 20 percent, but a docs-team reply on the community says you can type a larger number.
Small sources round. The value is rounded to the nearest whole account. If it rounds to less than one account, the aggregation is cancelled only when 100 percent of accounts would be deleted. At 5 percent on a 10-account source it rounds to one account, so any deletion cancels the run.

It applies to scheduled and flat-file aggregations too.
There is no built-in alert on a bulk status change such as many terminations. Community answers point to a workflow or a search-based monitor for that, which matches the monitors on the hypercare page.
A community case matches our concern exactly: a web-services source began returning an error with zero results and then deleted accounts. A low threshold (a few percent) was the suggested guard.
Optimized aggregation
By default, aggregation is optimized and skips unchanged accounts without re-running correlation. See the identity model page before you debug an uncorrelated account.
Scheduling facts
Frequencies are daily, every N, weekly and monthly. A daily recurrence ends at midnight, and monthly dates run from 1 to 28.
The schedule time zone follows the VA cluster setting, and schedules do not shift for daylight saving time. For a global program, write the time zone next to every schedule.

Queued or in-progress operations can delay the start of an aggregation.
Flat files
For best results keep flat files under 500 MB.
A delimited file should be sorted by account ID. Otherwise you can see one entitlement per account, because rows for the same account are not adjacent.
Without a connected VA, the flat file source is loaded by upload ("aggregate using latest file"), not by a schedule.

Rules are where most of the real integration logic lived on the program: 13 cloud rules and 41 connector rules. This page is the starting kit: which rule type to use, how to deliver one, and a template for each shape we used. The snippets are generalised from the program's rules with names, hosts and credentials removed. They show structure. Compile every one in the validator and test it on a sandbox source before use. Class and method names should be checked against the Javadoc for your tenant release.

| Cloud rule | Connector rule |
Runs | Inside ISC | On the virtual appliance, around a connector operation |
Network access | None | The connector's own managed client only |
Editable | By SailPoint, after review | Directly, through the connector-rule API |
Typical use | Compute a value, correlate, adjust a plan | Parse a response, build a request, talk to a database |
Review | Submitted to SailPoint, with the validator output. Most are reviewed within about a day | None |
Lives in | Source, identity profile or provisioning policy configuration | A source operation or a source attribute |
The review difference drives workflow. A cloud-rule change is a request with a lead time. A connector-rule change is an API call that takes effect on the next run, which makes it fast and dangerous.
Two places, two rules of the road. Cloud rules need SailPoint review and cannot call out. Connector rules are edited through the API and take effect on the next run.

Type | Purpose | Typical input | Returns |
Account profile attribute generator | Compute an account attribute when provisioning (a login name, an email) | The identity, the application, and the helper object | A value |
Identity attribute rule | Compute an identity attribute for the identity profile | The identity | A value |
Correlation rule | Match an account to an identity with logic a simple criterion cannot express | The account | A map naming the identity attribute and the value to match |
Before provisioning rule | Adjust the provisioning plan before it reaches the source | The plan, the identity, the application | Nothing (it edits the plan) |
Manager correlation rule | Work out an identity's manager | The account or identity | A map |
BuildMap rule | Reshape rows from a file | The row data | A map |
Transform rule | Used by a transform | The transform input | A value |
Variables seen in the program's rules: identity and application for generators and attribute rules, account for correlation, plan, application and identity for before-provisioning, and in all of them log and the helper idn.

Connector rule types
Type | Connector | Purpose | Variables seen |
Before operation | Web Services | Run before an HTTP operation: set the body, add a header, fetch a value | application, requestEndPoint, oldResponseMap, restClient, plus provisioningPlan on write operations. Returns the end point |
After operation | Web Services | Run after an HTTP operation: parse, reshape, set the disabled flag | application, requestEndPoint, processedResponseObject, rawResponseObject, restClient. Returns the list of accounts or groups |
BuildMap | JDBC | Turn each result row into an account map | result, schema. Returns the map |
JDBC provision | JDBC | Perform every write | plan, connection, application. Returns a provisioning result |
BuildMap | Delimited file | Reshape parsed file rows | the row data |
Before and after create, modify, delete | Active Directory | Run a script on the directory agent | (scripts run on the Windows host) |

SailPoint's documentation states that connector rules run on the appliance, receive managed connections from the platform, and that additional connections or call-outs are not allowed. On the program, web-services rules made calls through the connector's own client helper and that worked. Raw HTTP libraries did not (see the connectors pages). Treat any call a rule makes as a dependency and keep it to the connector's helper.

Cloud rules
One rule per use case, updated in place. Dozens of near-identical copies accumulated: four lifecycle-state variants and two next-processing-date variants sat in the tenant, with only one referenced. Keep the name plain and archive history in version control.
Controlled change window. SailPoint's guidance is to submit a -TEMP copy, validate it in the window, then update the original and ask for the temporary one to be deleted.
Submission standard. UTF-8, readable indentation, comments on non-obvious logic, no commented-out code, tested. Run the validator before you submit and attach its output.

Why these cases are hard
Pattern 1: dependent entitlements (role plus scope)
Pattern 2: cascading dropdowns that cascade
Pattern 3: getting data from the form into the rule
Pattern 4: composite access, read-modify-write

Choosing a pattern
A test matrix for complex requests
Actions
Most applications on the program were simple: a group, a person, a grant. A handful were not, and they consumed a disproportionate share of design, build and hypercare effort. This page collects the hard cases, the pattern that finally worked for each, and the traps that came with it. The applications are described by shape (the guide does not name internal systems), and we label them H, K, C and P so the cases can be referred to.

chunks.h: Complex Applications: Cascading Entitlements and Form-to-Rule Data
chunks.x:
Label | Shape | What made it hard |
H | A SQL Server application. Access is a role plus a scope (global, local office or client entity), stored as one row per role and entity | A grant is two dependent values, and ISC grants one entitlement at a time |
K | A REST application. Access is a list of composite access rows (service line, asset manager, client, region, country, entity, role) | No atomic "add one access" call, a cascade of five dependent fields, and entitlements that carry hidden identifiers |
C | A SQL Server application with one database per client | Users and groups live in many databases, so one source cannot aggregate them |
P | A payroll or HR product with a REST API and no group concept (two different products fall under this label) | Nothing to request, but revocation still has to do something, or an extra fact must be fetched before a write |

Four platform facts combine to make them hard:
An entitlement is one value on one attribute. A grant that needs a role and an entity is two entitlements, and nothing in the product says they belong together.
A provisioning plan carries attribute requests, not the form. By the time a connector rule runs, the answers the requester typed are not in the plan unless you carry them there.
Forms cannot cascade through a search over entitlement attributes. Entitlement attributes are not indexed, and data-source queries do not interpolate other fields (see the forms page).
Rules run on the appliance, one operation at a time. A rule sees one account request, with no memory of the one before it.
Every pattern below is a way of working around one or more of these.

The shape
Application H stores access as a row of user, role, entity. There are three scopes: global (a fixed entity), local office (an entity from an office table) and client entity (an entity from a client table). The same role means different things at each scope, so a grant is meaningless without both parts.
How it was modelled
Element | Choice |
Role | An entitlement on one attribute |
Entity | An entitlement on a second attribute per scope (one for local office, one for client entity) |
Removal | A third, composite attribute whose value is a pipe-delimited string carrying scope, entity and role |
Link between the two grants | Request comments holding the role and the entity, read by the provisioning rule |
Order | The workflow grants the role, waits one minute, then grants the entity |
The composite removal value is a contract. It looked like this (the format is illustrative):
text
```
GLOBAL ROLE | <role> | <extra>                      (three parts)
<scope> | <entity> | <role> | <extra>               (four parts)
```

The rule split on the delimiter and trusted the part count. A value with the wrong number of parts made the helper return the literal text Invalid format to its caller, a string and not an error. That is the failure mode of every name-encoded contract: a malformed value is not rejected, it is returned as if it were data. Make such helpers throw.
The grant sequence
text
```
Request form (scope, requestee, role[s])
   -> branch on scope
        Global:        for each role: grant role
        Local office:  for each role: grant role, wait 1 min, grant office entity
        Client entity: for each role: grant role, wait 1 min, grant client entity
   -> notify requester and requestee
```
Notes on the sequence:
The one-minute wait separates two provisioning events on the same account. The reason is our reading rather than something we measured: without it the second event can arrive while the first is still running on the same row. Treat the wait as a pragmatic concurrency guard and re-test it on your tenant.

Multiple roles multiply the loops. A role list with an entity list becomes a loop within a loop, and every loop body counts against the workflow's step limit. The design worked for a handful of selections and needed splitting beyond that.
The rule must prevent duplicates. The same role and entity can be granted twice by a retry or a second request, so the rule checks for an existing row before inserting.
Special roles may trigger side effects. In application H, three role identifiers also created report assignments. Document side effects in the integration notes, because they are invisible in ISC.
Dependent entitlements. Role and entity are separate grants. The one-minute wait separates two provisioning events on the same account.
The bug that taught the lesson
In sandbox testing, a global-scope grant was added even when the requester asked for a client-entity role. The program recorded the symptom and a before and after test of the fix, not the root cause, so treat the following as the lesson we drew rather than a diagnosis: the rule decides scope from request text, and any gap in that decision must not default to the broadest scope. Rules:

Never let the default branch of a scope decision grant access. Make it throw.
Test each scope as its own case, with a negative check that no other scope's row was written.
Keep the scope inside the data (Scope:Global) rather than inferring it.

A request form that offers scope, then client, then country, then entity needs each list to depend on the previous choice. A single form cannot do this. The pattern that worked uses several forms and a workflow, with the search API in between:
text
```
Form 1: choose scope and requestee
   -> workflow: search for valid parents using the chosen value
Form 2: choose from the filtered list (country)
   -> workflow: search for children using the chosen value
Form 3: choose from the next filtered list (entity), single or multiple
   -> workflow: grant
```
Multi-step forms. The only robust cascade on the platform: the workflow calls the search API between forms and builds each option list.
Making entitlements searchable by parent
Because entitlement attributes are not indexed, the parent must be stored in a field that is. The program used three:
Field | What it carried | Why it works |
description | The country an entity belongs to | Searchable and shown to users |

attribute | Which kind of entitlement it is (local office entity, client entity, global client) | Distinguishes the sets without parsing names |
tags | A normalised client name | Searchable, and independent of how the name is written |
A search for the entities of a chosen country and client then looks like this (placeholders in angle brackets):
text
```
description.exact:"<selected country>"
AND source.name.exact:"<source name>"
AND attribute.exact:"<client entity attribute>"
AND tags:"<normalised client>"
```
Normalising a value for a tag
Client names contain characters that break a query or a tag (&, -, spaces, brackets, full stops). The workflow strips them into a variable and uses the result as the tag:
text
```
Selected:    ACME & Partners (India).
Normalised:  ACMEPartnersIndia
```
Do this once, in one place, and apply the same rule when you create the tags. We found the normalisation repeated in two workflow branches with different capitalisation of the form field names, which is the kind of drift that makes one branch return nothing. Keep the tags and the workflow in step, and add a test that selects each client in each branch.

What to know before you build it
Every form and every loop counts. A four-level cascade with multi-select at two levels is a large workflow. Check it against the tier limit early.
An empty search result blocks a required field. If the entitlements have not been aggregated yet, the form cannot be submitted. Aggregate before the form goes live.
The Lucene list rendering trap applies. Build the query from strings, not from a list value.
Cap the list sizes. A parallel loop accepts at most 250 items.

chunks.h: Pattern 3: getting data from the form into the rule
chunks.x:
This is the question that came up on every complex application: the requester chose something on a form, and the connector rule needs it. The options, in the order we would try them:
Option | How | Strengths | Weaknesses |
A. Request comments | The workflow writes the selections as text or JSON into the comments of the access request. The rule reads them from the attribute request and clears them | Works inside the standard provisioning plan. No extra infrastructure | Only works when the request came through your workflow. Any other route (role, certification, API grant) arrives with no comments |
B. Encode it in the entitlement name | The value the user picks already carries the data, and the rule parses it | Survives every grant route, including certification remediation | The format is a contract. Renaming breaks every grant |
C. Write it to a staging table | The workflow writes a row (request id, user, selections) through a small API or database step, and the rule looks it up | Large or structured payloads, an audit trail | A second system to build and keep consistent |

chunks.h: Pattern 3: getting data from the form into the rule
chunks.x:
D. Call the target directly from the workflow | A web-services source operation is invoked by the workflow with the form data as the body | The rule is trivial or absent | Bypasses the plan, so ISC's view of the account lags until the next aggregation |
E. Fetch it live in the rule | The rule asks the target for the missing fact (a start date, a current access list) before building the request | Always current | Adds a network call to every operation and a failure mode to each |
Our practice: use A for a request-only grant, B for a value that must survive every route, E for facts the target already knows, and C when the payload is bigger than a comment.
Choosing a channel. Comments only exist for requests that came through your workflow; an entitlement name survives every route; a direct call skips the plan, so ISC's view lags until the next aggregation.
Option A in detail
The workflow's access-management step grants the access item and attaches the comment. For a role plus entity it holds something like this (format is yours to choose, keep it parseable):

chunks.h: Pattern 3: getting data from the form into the rule
Pattern 3: getting data from the form into the rule
chunks.x:
Comments are text. Escape quotes in names, and keep to one format across all rules in a source.
The symptom of a missing comment is a failed provisioning with METADATA IS NULL or similar. Put that string in your runbook.
Parsing a key:value string is fragile if a value contains a comma. JSON is safer.
Option E in detail: enrich in the rule
A before-operation rule can make its own call to fetch what the form did not collect. In one payroll product integration, the request body for an add-entitlement needed the employee's start date, which the plan did not carry. The rule fetched the employee record, read the start date, and built the body from the entitlement value plus that date. The same idea derived a hidden field in application K from the client and service line. Two cautions:
Fail clearly when the lookup returns nothing. Submitting an empty array, or a null date, creates a silent bad write.

chunks.h: Pattern 3: getting data from the form into the rule
chunks.x: Never put credentials in the rule to make the call. An early version did, and it is one of the findings on the security page. Use the source's own connection.
Application K stores access as a list of rows, and its API offered no "add one row". The only safe write is: read the current list, merge the new rows, write the whole list back. ```html

text
```

Consequences for the design:

| Concern | Design response |
|---|---|
| Two requests for the same user at once | The second write can overwrite the first. Serialise requests per user, or re-read and compare before writing |
| A row for several identities | An outer loop over identities, the same rows for each |
| A failure for one identity | Record it, continue the loop, and report partial failure in the final notification |
| Proof it worked | A read-back step compares what the application now holds with what was asked |
| A hidden dependency (a level-2 service list) | Derived in a before-operation rule from the client and service line, never asked of the requester |
…
```
Granularity: one row, one level
Application K keeps one granularity per row: a row holds regions, or countries, or entities, never a mix. Coarser lists are derived from finer ones. Sending a coarse list on a row that already holds a finer one is silently discarded with a success response. Therefore:

A country-scoped grant cannot be merged into a row that holds an entity. It needs its own row.
Key the rows by service line, client and level, not by service line and client alone.
Several rows per service line and client is correct. The union of a person's rows is what they can reach.
This is a general rule worth remembering: when an API accepts a value and returns success, read it back before you believe it.

chunks.h: Pattern 5: entitlement values that carry identifiers
chunks.x:
Application K needed two internal identifiers to revoke a grant, and ISC's entitlement had only a name. The program packed them into the display name:
text
```
<role> [>> <client>] >> <service line> ((<access row id>::<role id>))
```
The revoke rules parse the two ids back out. Consequences:
Changing the format renames every entitlement and detaches every grant, so revoke must be changed in the same release.
A malformed or missing segment means the grant cannot be resolved. It is the first thing to check when a revoke reports success and the target did not change.
The target may re-mint the id when a grant is edited. The old entitlement value vanishes and a new one appears, so entitlement counts move between aggregations. That is the target's behaviour, not an ISC fault.
Entitlements nobody holds do not exist, if the source has no group aggregation. ISC cannot list the catalogue.
The revoke rule should read the live state of the target first, because the aggregated view may be months old. That makes revoke correct even when aggregation is stale.

Application C holds users and groups in a separate database per client, and a JDBC source reaches one database. The solution was a centralised integration database:
Piece | Role |
A central database | Receives users and entitlements consolidated from every client database |
A client-to-database mapping table | Holds which database belongs to which client |
One ISC source | Aggregates accounts and groups from the central database only |
The mapping, aggregated as entitlement | So the request form can offer a client and ISC knows its database |
A stored procedure | Accepts the user, the group and the target database name, and writes to the right client database |
The provisioning rule | Reads group and client from the request comment, looks up the database name, calls the procedure |
Why this was better than one source per database: it needed one source, one schedule and one runbook instead of dozens. The costs are a job that keeps the central database in step with the client databases, and a stored procedure the application team must own.
Central integration database. One source, one schedule and one runbook instead of one source per database. The cost is the sync job and a procedure the application team must own.

chunks.h: Pattern 8: multi-valued updates and operation rewriting
chunks.x:
Two smaller rules recur:
Replace-only connectors. Some connectors have no native add or remove for a multi-valued attribute and no single-account read, so they only support replace. A before-provisioning cloud rule can turn each "add" or "remove" into a "set": read the account's current values from ISC, add or remove the requested values, and send the whole list. Skip create and delete requests, check the schema says the attribute is multi-valued, and return quietly when there is nothing to do. This is the same read-modify-write idea as pattern 4, done in a rule.
Operation rewriting. A before-provisioning rule can change a disable into a move, an enable into a re-enable with attributes, or strip entitlements before a leaver move. Keep the logic table-driven if you can, so the next change is a configuration edit and not a code edit.

Your situation | Start with |
A grant needs two dependent values | Pattern 1, with an explicit scope and a composite value for removal |
The form needs lists that depend on earlier choices | Pattern 2 (multi-step forms), with the parent stored in a searchable field |
A rule needs something the requester chose | Pattern 3, option A, then B or C if it must survive other routes |
The API only offers "replace the whole list" | Pattern 4, with read-back and per-user serialisation |
You must parse an identifier out of an entitlement | Pattern 5, and freeze the format |
Data lives in many databases | Pattern 6 |
The application has no groups | Pattern 7 |

chunks.h: A test matrix for complex requests
chunks.x:
Build this before the first UAT. Each row is one test with a before and after check on the target:
Case | Check |
Each scope, single role, single entity | The right rows and no others |
Each scope, several roles, several entities | The full cross product, once |
Duplicate request | No duplicate row |
Request through a route that carries no comment | A clear failure, not a wrong write |
Revoke each scope | The right row removed, nothing else |
Format change smoke test | Add, request, complete, revoke and certify before and after |
One identity failing in a multi-identity request | Others succeed, failure reported |
Two concurrent requests for one user | No lost update |
Entitlement not yet aggregated | The form states a useful message |
Target returns success but changes nothing | The read-back catches it |

Describe each complex application as a pattern (this page), not as a one-off, so the next one starts from a known design.
Decide how form data reaches the rule before you build the form, and write down which routes will not carry it.
Store the parent of every dependent value in a searchable field, and test each branch of a cascade.
Treat every parsed name format as an API: freeze it, test it and version it.
Make the default branch of any scope decision an error.
Read back after every write to an API that can return success without acting.
Put the failure strings (METADATA IS NULL, Invalid format) in the runbook.

chunks.h: Forms, Launchers and Workflows: Limits and Workarounds
chunks.x:
SailPoint ISC Greenfield Implementation Field Guide
On this page
How the pieces fit
Forms: what works and what does not
Workflows: engine limits and behaviour
Design patterns that worked
Workflow health: what to monitor
What SailPoint's documentation adds
Actions
Forms, launchers and workflows are how you build anything the standard Request Center cannot do: composite requests, manager questionnaires, lifecycle emails, HR writeback. They are also where the platform's sharpest edges are. Most of what follows was measured in a sandbox tenant while building form-driven flows, and it applies to any flow you build. Re-test before relying on a limit, because the engine changes.

A form on its own is not reachable by anyone. The working chain is:
A launcher (type interactive process) appears in the user's launchpad.
It starts a workflow whose trigger is "interactive process launched", filtered on that workflow's own ID.
The workflow's first step is an interactive form.
The form's answers come back inline as $.interactiveForm.formData.
Later steps act: look up identities, call APIs, raise approvals, manage access, send mail.
Launcher visibility: creating a launcher auto-creates an entitlement on the internal ISC source (attribute assignedLaunchers), non-requestable. Make it requestable and grant it (or grant it through a role) before anyone sees a Launch button. The button enables only when the launcher is assigned and its workflow is enabled. Launchers cannot be patched (405); the owner on create is overridden by the API client.
A usedBy: MySailPoint marker on a form is only a usage marker. Writing it launches nothing.
The working chain. Creating a launcher auto-creates a non-requestable entitlement; grant it directly or through a role before anyone sees the button.

chunks.h: Forms: what works and what does not
chunks.x:
Dependent dropdowns cannot cascade
A search data source on a form cannot filter one dropdown by another dropdown's selection. Two independent reasons:
Entitlement attributes are not indexed. The search index returns null for them; only name, value, attribute, schema and source are queryable. A flag stored as an entitlement attribute (for example a Read or Write marker) cannot drive a filter.
Values containing hyphens tokenise, so wildcard prefix queries on them do not work.
Also: data-source queries do not interpolate form values. Six reference syntaxes against four body shapes returned zero options while a literal returned one.
Workarounds that worked:
Workaround | How |
Put the context in the display name | Asia · Client · A&T, or (Read Only) and (Write) suffixes on profile names |
Put the context in entitlement tags | Query tags with a Lucene OR such as tags:("A" "B") |
Multi-step interactive forms | The solution that delivered true cascading: the first form collects a value, the workflow calls the Search API with that value, builds the option list, and presents it in the next form. Repeat for each dependent level. A group, then role, then client selection on one SQL application used this |

chunks.h: Forms: what works and what does not
chunks.x:
Progressive disclosure | Hide a child field until the parent is chosen (using empty or not-empty conditions), without filtering its options |
Hard-code a short list | If only two groups are ever requestable, say so in the query and accept that adding one is a query edit |
Multi-step forms are slower and heavier on the workflow tier limit but they are the only robust way to cascade.
Conditions and effects
A condition or effect whose rule reads a form input did nothing (show, hide, default value, require). Rules on form elements work. Rebuilding with 26 inputs instead of 130 changed nothing, so it is not a size limit. One approval form fed by a workflow form step did honour input-sourced conditions, so verify in a browser before relying on it for a new field.
SHOW works on a section, not an element, so invert show rules into hides.
Section labels are not rendered by the launcher. Put anything the user must see in a field label.

chunks.h: Forms: what works and what does not
chunks.x:
Operators EQ, CO, NOT_CO, IN, NOT_IN, SW, EW accept string or boolean only. A string list works only with empty and not-empty. NOT_EQ, GT, LT, INCLUDES, ANY, ALL are rejected.
A string rule reading a multi-select is rejected at submit (must be a string).
There is no native repeatable group. Use fixed blocks revealed by conditions, or loop over a multi-select in the workflow.
Conditions address elements by numeric element ID, not key. Preserve the IDs when editing a form or the prefill and lock silently stop working.
A casing trap: the form input may be userSailpointId and the element userSailPointId. Submitted data is keyed by element. Anything downstream must read the element's casing.
Reading what someone submitted
Launcher-driven forms leave formData: {} in the execution history. The answers live only on the form instance, and only the instance list returns formData; a GET by ID does not. Use the list when you need to see what a user entered.

chunks.h: Forms: what works and what does not
chunks.x:
Do not delete a form a launch may still point at
Retire it. A launch in flight that holds a deleted form definition fails with HTTP 404 at submit time, and the submission cannot be recovered. This was learned by breaking a colleague's open request.

Secrets and credentials
Literal secrets written through the API are silently dropped. Writing an OAuth client secret as a plain value stores empty and the runtime receives an empty string. Read-back of an empty string looks identical to masking, so you only find out by executing.
The secret reference convention is produced only by the UI. There is no secrets API. Any workflow that needs credentials has a mandatory human step.
A full-object PUT wipes a UI-set secret unless you read back and preserve the reference. This is the easiest way to break a working workflow through the API: edit it, lose both secrets, and the HTTP steps fail authentication.
ISC pins one OAuth parameter reference per workflow. A new step strips the reference; an update overwrites all references with one shared value; a shared reference fails with failed to retrieve Parameters for authentication type 'oauth'. If a workflow has two HTTP steps with different credentials, it is fragile.

Our HR writeback workflows put the client secret and grant in plaintext in the HTTP body. Do not copy that. Create the secret in the UI and reference it.
Templating and data
Behaviour | Consequence |
An unresolvable template path renders as literal {{...}} text | Never an error, never empty. A truncated field name corrupted a payload silently |
.JSON() is the only stringify function | .String(), .Quote(), .ToString(), .JSONEscape() render literally |
A list renders like [5 2] | tags:([236 201]) is an HTTP 400 Lucene error. tags:("A" "B") works as OR |
Define Variable and Update Variable allow at most 50 operations per variable (documented) | Plan grouping |
sp:access:get returns {id, name, type} only, no value | Use an HTTP search step when you need the value |
sp:http v3 returns the raw API response including value | v2 hung forever |
There is no "create account" action | sp:manage-account only touches existing accounts. Creation goes through POST /accounts, which runs the connector's create operation and its before-rules. Linkage to an identity is by correlation only |

Loops
Inside a loop the current item is $.loop.loopInput; things outside the loop are $.loop.context...; a sibling step inside the loop sits at the root.
A loop over an empty or absent input completes cleanly with zero iterations, so no guard step is needed.
Inner loop steps do not appear in the parent execution history. An approval step inside a loop cannot be debugged from the parent execution.
Limits and validation
Tier limits count loop bodies, not top-level steps. A workflow with 36 steps across 24 loops enabled; one with 49 steps across 35 loops was rejected with Tier Limit Violation: Your workflow must have 50 or fewer steps after the trigger.
Validation runs on enable, not on save. A PUT returns 200 with invalid content; the error appears when you enable. Step display names must be under 65 characters.
You cannot PUT an enabled workflow. Disable it, PUT, enable it again.
sp:generic-approval was not licensed. It saved and then failed on enable. Approval had to be form-based: an sp:forms step blocks and returns the form data inline.

sp:interactive-form does not reliably raise sp:form-submitted. Do not build a second workflow on that event for a request form. Trigger the execution workflow on the approval form instead.
Triggers
Trigger | Notes |
Identity attributes changed | Filter by attribute name and new value with JSONPath. Fires per change |
Post-provisioning | Filter on committed result, target source and operation |
Form submitted | Filter by form definition ID; keep the ID in sync if you recreate the form |
Schedule | Has its own time zone |
External HTTP | Used for welcome emails; authenticates with a client ID |
Useful property: workflow executions are kept, and the dump of 250 executions per workflow gave a quick health read (completed, failed, canceled, executing).
Operational traps found the hard way
A 63-second VA timeout wedges the requester for about an hour. Every later request from the same identity returns CANCELLED. It affects only that person and looks exactly like a rule fault. Two submissions in a row by one requester will show the second as cancelled.

A workflow with a Wait step leaves executions in Executing for as long as it waits. A large count is normal; a growing count of Canceled needs explaining.
The same workflow in sandbox and production must have different recipients. Mail steps with hard-coded addresses are the commonest promotion defect.
Email recipients: fix them to identities from the flow, not one named person. Our request workflow sent approvals and rejections to one fixed address, so the requester and the beneficiary were never told.

A launcher flow with per-item approval
For a request that names several clients: a loop over the multi-select raises one approval form instance per client (with a deadline), and each submission fires an execution workflow separately. Properties to document for users:
There is no bundling. Three approvals and one rejection yields three grants.
A deadline that expires is silent. "Never appeared" and "expired" look the same to the requester.
The group dropdown was a hard-coded query for two names. Adding a third is a query edit.
Form visibility came from a criteria role, so the tile appears and disappears on identity refresh with no record explaining why.
Event plus sweep
Pair every event-triggered workflow that must not miss work with a scheduled sweep (HR writeback, GreytHR disable, leaver off-boarding). Events are lost; a sweep repairs them.
Execution workflow triggered by an approval form
Because sp:interactive-form is unreliable for raising a submitted event, split the work: the request workflow collects and raises approval forms; a second workflow triggers on the approval form's submission and does the provisioning. Keep the execution workflow and the provisioning rule as one unit (they share the comments-channel contract; see the connector deep dive).

Dead steps and duplicate searches
A review of one production workflow found: two near-identical search steps (one matching an analysed field, one an exact field) feeding different values, so the database name and the entitlement ID could come from different entitlements; a variable step nobody read; and a replace pattern with a truncated field name. Use the exact match, delete the other, and review the workflow end to end after every edit.

Failed execution count and rate, per workflow, per week.
Executions stuck in Executing past the expected wait.
Enabled flag on every workflow that should be enabled (the tenant had 28, 21 enabled, with several test and copy workflows).
Test and copy workflows should be deleted, not left disabled. Ours included copies of the joiner flows, a manually triggered joiner and leaver, and two test workflows.

Checked against the workflows documentation, the operators page and the community announcement of serial loops, October 2026.
Topic | Documented position |
Volume | Up to 400,000 executions per day run at full speed. Beyond that they still run, at about 5 per second. The quota resets every 24 hours |
First use | After workflows are first enabled in a tenant, allow up to two hours before the feature is fully working. Errors during that time are expected |
Structure | Exactly one trigger per workflow and at least one action |
Permissions | Org Admin configures workflows. Two read-only roles exist: one cannot see execution history, the other can |
Parallel loop | Input array of at most 250 items. More fails the workflow |
Serial loop | A newer operator with input of at most 1,000 items. An iteration that fails stops the loop. A Break Loop operator exists. In test mode the loop is limited to 50 iterations |

Define Variable | At most 50 operations per variable |
Add Time | The result cannot be more than a year from the original date |
Notes for the design:
The 50-step tier limit we hit is plan-dependent. Community posts quote different step allowances by licence level, so read the limit off your own tenant error rather than from this guide, and re-check after a plan change.
Older community threads describe loop limits of 100 items. That predates the current operators. Check the date on any limit you find.
A serial loop is the right choice when order matters, when one failure should stop the rest, or when you need more than 250 items. A parallel loop completes every iteration and lists successes and failures separately, which suits independent items. Our observation that inner loop steps do not appear in the parent execution history was measured on the parallel loop; check whether serial loops differ.
There is no documented per-execution timeout or workflow-level retry. Community designs build retries by hand with a counter in a serial loop.

Design the request experience around the cascade limit before you build forms.
Create workflow secrets in the UI, by a named person, and document where.
Count loop steps against the tier limit during design.
Keep an inventory of workflows, forms, launchers and the IDs that tie them together.
Retire, never delete, forms with launches in flight.
