Go-live is where the work changes shape: the build team stops writing and starts reading tickets. This page covers what the issue log looked like in the weeks after cutover, the operating routine the runbooks settled on, the monitors worth building, and how knowledge was handed to the team that would run the platform.

The issue log from hypercare held about 75 rows. They fell into a small number of families, and almost none were about the core engine failing. They were about data, notifications and edge cases around people.
Category | Typical issue | Likely cause (our reading of the log) |
Re-add directory groups | A person lost a group and wanted it back | Role criteria changed, or a mover flow removed access |
Display name issues | Wrong or inconsistent name in the directory | HR name fields, or a transform that cleaned them |
Rehire account issues | A returning employee had an old account or a duplicate | Rehire path not fully covered by the joiner logic |
Contact update | Phone or address stale after an HR change | The attribute feeding the lookup was not refreshed |
Form and notification issues | The manager never got the form. Credentials mail went to the wrong person. Nobody could see whether a form had been completed | Routing by role, manager changes, no visibility of form state |

Re-assignment | A form had to be resent to a new manager | The original approver left or changed |
Email update | Work email needed pushing back to HR | Writeback gaps |
Disable access | A leaver's end date in HR was wrong | HR data, not ISC |
New account creation (old process) | Someone asked for an account through the legacy route | Change management and communication |
Duplicate identifiers in the directory | Duplicate distinguished name or user principal name | Name collision handling |
Finance consolidation tool | Read-only and legacy groups had no access profiles | Fixed by creating an "Others" application for leftover access |
General access | A profile was missing or not requestable | Access model gaps |
The log also recorded two program risks that persisted: the approval step for the most sensitive client system had been removed, and integration credentials were held in a vault that administrators download tokens from locally.

Lessons from the pattern
Most tickets are data or routing, not code. Staff the first weeks with people who can read HR data and mailbox rules, not only developers.
Notifications are the biggest source of noise. Seven notification changes were made after go-live. Draw the matrix of template, trigger, recipient and fallback before go-live, and review it with the service desk.
Give people visibility. "Did my manager complete the form?" is a question the platform does not answer by default. Decide who can see form state and how.
Rehires are a whole flow, not a joiner variant. Write test cases for them in UAT.
A reassignment path is a requirement. Approvers leave. A form that cannot be resent to a new manager becomes a manual task for the team.
Leftover access needs a home. The "Others" application absorbed security groups nobody had modelled.

The per-integration runbooks converged on the same structure, and it is a good template for your own.
Schedule calendar
A table of every aggregation, every lifecycle job and every report, with time zone. A global deployment ran across four time zones, so write the zone down.
Health checks
Check | How |
Freshness | The last aggregation date per source, from a search over a lastAggregationDate attribute. Alert when older than the schedule plus a margin |
Disabled count | A search for disabled accounts per source, compared to yesterday |
Delete threshold | Confirm the configured value did not change |
Uncorrelated list | Count and review the accounts with no identity |
Entitlement count | A sudden halving means a truncated aggregation (see the page limit on listing) |
Sentinel literal | A search for a placeholder such as a computed-by-rule marker that should never appear in a real value |
Cluster status | Every VA healthy, no cluster down to one appliance |

Troubleshooting by symptom
Each runbook has a table that maps a symptom to a likely cause, a way to confirm, and a fix. The generalised version is on the last page of this guide.
Making a change safely
A checklist, in this order: read the current configuration, take a backup or export, change in sandbox first, test one object before many, deploy, verify with a search, record the change. Include "update the lifecycle state source list" for any new source, and "update the runbook".
Read-only API recipes
A list of GET calls an on-call engineer can run without risk, with the filters to use. They are also on the last page.

The platform will not alert on most of the quiet failures. Build monitors for:
Monitor | Why |
Population count per aggregation run | A truncated feed shows as a sudden drop |
Status counts per source (enabled, disabled, locked) | A broken status comparison makes every account look enabled |
Age of last aggregation per source | Two production sources ran for months without a schedule |
Failed and cancelled workflow rates | A rising rate means a downstream system changed |
Cluster status | A VA down to one appliance is a risk before it is an outage |
Delete threshold audit | A threshold edited during troubleshooting and left behind |
Test and copy workflow clean-up | They are live objects |
Rule inventory | New or changed rules since last review |

The delivery team will leave, so knowledge transfer was treated as a deliverable with its own acceptance.
The documentation pack
For every integration, five files and a redacted configuration folder:
File | Holds |
README | What it is, who owns it, status, links |
01 Integration | How it works end to end: endpoints or queries, rules, workflows, mapping |
02 Tenant context | The objects in the tenant that belong to this integration, their names and settings |
03 Edge cases and dead ends | What was tried and did not work, so nobody repeats it |
04 Runbook | Schedule, health checks, symptoms, change procedure, API recipes |
config/ | Redacted exports of the source, rules, workflows and forms |
The "dead ends" file is the most valuable and the one teams skip. It saves the next engineer days.
The closure document
A closure document template covered the handover to the run team: scope delivered, open items, known issues, risks, support model, contacts and acceptance. Treat acceptance as a signature, not as an assumption.

Acceptance checklist for run
Run team has read access to the tenant and has used it to run the health checks.
Every runbook has been exercised once by someone who did not write it.
Open issues and risks are in a log with owners.
Credentials are owned and have a rotation plan.
Support model is written: who is first line, what is second line, when ISC support is called.

Decide before go-live:
First line answers "how do I" and routes tickets. Give them the FAQ and a short decision tree.
Second line can read the tenant and run the health checks and recipes.
Third line can change rules, workflows and sources. Limit this to a few named people.
Vendor support for platform problems and for rule changes that cannot be made in the tenant.
An ITSM queue, assignment group and mailbox should exist before go-live, along with membership for the integrator, so that the first ticket does not wait on access.

Staff hypercare for data and routing problems, not just defects.
Build the notification matrix before go-live and review it with the service desk.
Create the monitors above on day one, especially freshness and status counts.
Produce the five-file pack per integration, including the dead ends, and have a person who did not write each one run its runbook.
Define the support model and open the ITSM routes before cutover.
Keep an issue log with a category column; the pattern in it is your backlog.

Every implementation ends with the people who built it leaving. In ISC that departure is not an HR formality, because the platform ties objects, credentials, notifications and knowledge to named individuals. When those individuals are disabled or removed, workflows can stop, approvals can stall, sources can lose their owner, scripts can lose their tokens and the runbook can turn out to live in someone's head. This page describes what the tenant looked like at the end of the program, what breaks and why, and a sequence for leaving a platform that keeps working. Counts are rounded or exact from a read-only tenant dump, and no names appear.

chunks.h: Why this is a platform risk
chunks.x:
An ISC object is rarely independent of a person. Four kinds of tie exist:
Tie | Example | What it does when the person goes |
Ownership | The owner of a source, a workflow, an access profile, a role, a form | The object has no accountable owner. Some objects block the person's deletion. Some lose their notifications |
Credential | A workflow's personal access token, a token a script uses | The credential is disabled or invalid, and whatever uses it fails |
Routing | An approver, a governance group member, a hard-coded email address, a certification reviewer | Work is sent to someone who no longer reads it |
Knowledge | A script, a runbook that exists only locally, a vault entry only one person can open | The next person cannot reproduce or repair what was built |
The implementation team is the worst case, because it created most of the platform and holds a disproportionate share of all four.
Four ties. The same person usually appears in all four, which is why offboarding an implementer is a project and not a ticket. Figures are from the final tenant snapshot.

At the end of the program the tenant held the following. The dump is a snapshot from the final weeks.
Object type | Count | Concentration |
Workflows | 28 | 25 owned by one person, 3 by another |
Sources | 146 | Two people owned 109 of them (about three quarters) |
Access profiles | 3,333 | One person owned about 3,050 (over 90 percent) |
Roles | 284 | Two people owned 272 |
Campaign templates | 519 | Four people owned 483 |
Governance groups | 45 | Owned by a handful of individuals. 27 groups had one or two members, 4 had one |
Saved searches | 87 | Three people owned 84 |
Scheduled searches | 5 | Two owners. Searches were also the source of the nightly joiner and leaver exports |
Personal access tokens | 10 | Each tied to an individual. Six shared one expiry date, four had not been used for over three months |
OAuth clients | 14 | Nine belonged to the appliances. Five served integrations (webhooks, a leaver search, external workflow triggers, a form portal) |

Workflow email addresses | 54 literal addresses | 43 looked like shared mailboxes or lists, 11 looked personal |
Org-wide approval settings | | No fallback approver, no reminders, no escalation |
Three things stand out.
Ownership was concentrated. One identity owned nine in ten access profiles and most workflows. That is typical of a build done by a small team, and it is exactly what makes the departure dangerous.
Credentials were personal. The tokens were created by individuals, and several were the sort of convenience credential (a script, an editor extension, a REST client) that outlives its purpose.
There was no safety net. With no fallback approver and no reminders, an approval addressed to a removed person simply waits. The same is true of a certification.
The administrator identities, too, came from a small delimited file with no appliance, not from the HR feed. Identities loaded that way are not touched by the HR leaver automation. Offboarding the implementers' own administrator accounts is a manual task unless you plan it.

Object | What happens when the owner is disabled or removed | Impact |
Workflow | The admin who creates a workflow becomes its owner and gets a personal access token for it. If that owner leaves, SailPoint's documentation calls the workflow orphaned: it has no owner and its token becomes invalid, and executions can fail with unauthorised errors. Community reports say steps such as Get Identity and Manage Access run with the owner's permissions, so joiner, mover and leaver flows are the first to suffer | Highest. The automation that provisions and disables people stops, usually without an obvious alarm |
Source | A source must have an owner. The owner cannot be deleted while they own it. A source reset is blocked if any source owner holds an account on the source. The owner is also who reviews uncorrelated accounts in source-owner campaigns | High for operations and reviews |
Access profile, role, application | An identity that owns any of these cannot be deleted. Where the profile's approval is "owner", the approval goes to someone who is gone | High where owner approval is used. Silent elsewhere |

Entitlement | The owner is used for review and approval routing. Entitlement owners are often forgotten | Medium |
Governance group | Members vanish from approvals and reviews. A group of one becomes an empty group | High. 4 groups had a single member |
Campaign and template | Notifications go to the template owner. A reviewer who is removed leaves items waiting. An identity that is a reviewer of an active certification cannot be deleted | High around review cycles |
Form and launcher | Forms carry an owner. Forms are tied to workflows by identifier. We did not find a documented rule for what a form does when its owner is removed, so treat it as a risk to test | Medium. Unverified |
Saved and scheduled search | Scheduled searches are owned. Whether they keep running after the owner is disabled depends on release, so test it. The program's nightly joiner and leaver exports were scheduled searches | Medium to high. Monitoring goes quiet |

Personal access token | Belongs to the creating user and cannot exceed their access. Community reports say tokens are disabled when the identity is disabled, revoking bearer tokens immediately, and that re-enabling the identity does not bring them back. A token that a script, a pipeline or a campaign tool uses stops working | High for automation |
API client (OAuth) | Documented as not tied to a person. A client used by a workflow's external trigger or a webhook keeps working. Review what each client can do (scopes) and who knows its secret | Medium. The secret and the knowledge of it matter |
Appliance clients | Created for the virtual appliances, independent of people | Low |
Notification, approval, escalation settings | Hard-coded addresses, approvers by identifier, and an empty fallback approver mean mail and work go to inactive recipients | High where addressed to a person |
Admin user levels and MFA | Administrator accounts need MFA. A shared or service administrator whose authenticator lives on one person's phone is a person-dependent credential | High, and discovered at the worst time |

Disable and delete are different
From SailPoint's identity documentation:
Disabling an identity removes sign-in to the platform immediately. An active session continues until it ends. It does not disable the person's accounts in source systems or revoke access there. User levels are kept.
Deleting an identity removes its correlated accounts from the identity (they are not deprovisioned at the source). Identities that own sources, roles, access profiles or applications cannot be deleted, nor can reviewers of active certifications. Assign new owners and reassign the reviews first.
A deletion is only temporary if the person still exists in an authoritative source, because the next aggregation can recreate the identity with a new internal identifier. The person then has to be invited again and given back any elevated rights.
So the order is: reassign everything, then disable, then observe, then delete if you must.

Credentials the team knows. Source credentials and client secrets that only the implementers have seen. Workflow secrets can only be created in the UI, so a rotation needs a person who can do it and has the vault.
Local material. Tenant dumps, exported rules and workflows, scripts and workbooks on laptops, some containing credentials. These must be found, handed over or destroyed. The campaign tool's workbook holds an API client and a file server login.
Tokens in tools. Editor extensions, REST clients and scripts each held a token. Unused tokens are not harmless: they are valid until expiry.
Several tokens expiring together. Six tokens carried the same expiry date, which suggests a bulk update. They will all stop on the same day, and whoever remembers them will have left.
Support and vendor channels. Support cases, expert services contacts, community accounts, the ITSM queue the integrator joined, mailing lists and chat channels.

Approvals and notifications addressed to individuals. Eleven personal-looking addresses sat in workflow definitions, and the approval fallback was empty.
Hard-coded identifiers. Workflows reference objects by identifier. Rebuilding or transferring them changes those identifiers.
Service desk ownership. Who now answers "the manager never got the form" at two in the morning.
Contract ends but access does not. Implementation accounts in downstream systems (directories, the ITSM tool, application consoles) are not removed by ISC. Offboard them in those systems.
Support access. SailPoint's own support and services tokens are removed when tenant access expires. Re-grant it deliberately if you will need help.

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
A sequence, not an event. Dates are relative to the departure. Start the inventory three months out; the reassignments are the long pole.
1. Inventory (about 90 days before)
Build an owner register: every object, its type, its owner, a deputy and a review date. Produce it from the API, not from memory. The script below groups by owner and writes a file you can review.
python
```

TOKEN = os.environ["ISC_TOKEN"]
BASE = f"https://{TENANT}.api.identitynow.com"

# path, name of the owner field in the response (names differ by object type; check each)
ENDPOINTS = [
    ("/v2025/sources", "owner"),
    ("/v2025/access-profiles", "owner"),
    ("/v2025/roles", "owner"),
    ("/v2025/workflows", "owner"),
    ("/v2025/form-definitions", "owner"),
    ("/v2025/governance-groups", "owner"),
    ("/v2025/campaign-templates", "ownerRef"),
    ("/v2025/saved-searches", "ownerId"),
    ("/v2025/scheduled-searches", "ownerId"),
]

def get(path, offset=0, limit=250):
…

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
Notes: some endpoints do not take limit and offset, and some are in the beta namespace, so check each against the current API reference. Add the personal access tokens (listed per owner by an administrator), the OAuth clients and the scheduled searches' recipients. Sort the result by owner and count objects per departing person: that count is your effort estimate.
Also search the definitions for hard-coded addresses and identifiers:
bash
```
grep -rnoE "[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2,}" exported-workflows/ | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
grep -rnoE "\b[0-9a-f]{32}\b" exported-workflows/ | cut -d: -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```
2. Design the target ownership model (about 75 days before)
Object | Owner after the handover | Why |
Workflows and their tokens | A dedicated, non-expiring administrator identity (a service identity), with its authenticator held by named people | SailPoint's guidance is to create workflows with an administrator account that will not expire, and community practice is a service identity |

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
Sources | The platform team lead as technical owner, with the application owner as business contact | Source ownership drives operational notices and uncorrelated-account reviews |
Access profiles and roles | The application owner or a governance group, never a person on a project | Ownership of thousands of objects must not sit with one person |
Governance groups | At least three named members, from different teams | A group of one is an outage waiting for a holiday |
Campaign templates | A governance group or the compliance function | Reviews outlive the project |
Forms and launchers | The service identity | They are tied to workflows |
Saved and scheduled searches | The service identity, with recipients as a shared mailbox | They are monitors |
Tokens and clients | One per integration, owned by the service identity, with the least scope that works, an expiry, and a named human owner in the register | Credentials need an accountable owner that is not the creator |

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
Notifications | Shared mailboxes and lists, never individuals | Mail should survive a departure |
Approvals | A fallback approver, reminders and an escalation | A missing person should delay a request, not strand it |
The service identity must be governed: record who holds its credentials and its multi-factor authenticator, keep break-glass credentials with named people, and review it quarterly. Some of the community material suggests the platform's service-account approach is being superseded by newer machine identity features, so confirm what your release recommends.
3. Reassign (about 60 to 30 days before)
Transfer in this order, testing after each group:
Governance groups: add members first, then change owners.
Access profiles, roles, entitlements, applications. Use the list endpoints filtered by owner and update the owner. Do it in bulk, scripted, with a before and after count.
Sources. Change the owner on each. Check that none of the owners is also an account holder on a source you will reset.

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
Workflows. A workflow must be disabled before its owner is changed. Assigning it to another administrator generates a new personal access token and a new owner. Do one at a time, run it, check an execution.
Forms, launchers, saved and scheduled searches. Transfer, then verify that a scheduled search still produces its output and its recipients still receive it.
Campaign templates and active certifications. Reassign reviews and templates. Complete or reassign active campaigns before disabling a reviewer.
Tokens and clients. Create replacements under the service identity, switch each consumer, confirm it works, then revoke the old one. Record the new expiry.
The community has built workflows that react to a leaver by finding what the person owned and asking the manager for a new owner. Useful ideas, but note their limits (loop caps, search index lag) and that workflow reassignment may reassign requests, not ownership. Test them. There is also a product connector designed for governance reassignments, which may fit if you want this to be permanent.

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
4. Make it repeatable (about 30 days before)
Keep the owner register current, with a quarterly review.
Add a monitor for objects whose owner is inactive, disabled or missing. A search for identities with an inactive lifecycle state that still own things is the simplest one.
Add a monitor for workflow execution failures with authorisation errors.
Add a monitor for tokens approaching expiry or not used for a long time.
Schedule the reassign automation if you use it.
5. Shadow period (about 30 days before)
Have the receiving team run the platform while the implementers are still there. They should exercise every runbook (the hypercare page lists them) and make one real change safely each. Use the findings to correct the documentation.
6. Disable, observe, then delete (cutover and the 30 days after)
Disable the identities, do not delete them. Disabling stops sign-in and (according to community reports) their tokens, but it does not touch their accounts at source systems, so offboard those in the directories and applications themselves.

chunks.h: A sequence that keeps the platform running
chunks.x:
Observe for 30 days. Watch the workflow failure rate, scheduled search output, joiner and leaver volumes, aggregation freshness, and approvals waiting.
Delete only when nothing owns anything, no active certifications name them, and the owner register shows no references. Remember a person who is still in an authoritative source can reappear as a new identity.
Remove vendor access: support cases, expert services, community and chat memberships, the ITSM queue.

Treat the handover as a deliverable with a signature, not an assumption.
Check | Evidence |
Owner register delivered and reconciled with the tenant | The register matches a fresh export |
No object owned by a departing person | A zero-row owner query |
Workflows run under the service identity | An execution after reassignment succeeds |
Tokens and clients rotated | Old ones revoked, new expiry dates recorded |
Secrets and authenticator custody documented | Who holds them, and a tested recovery |
Runbooks exercised by the receiving team | A signed log of each exercise |
Local material accounted for | A list of dumps, scripts and workbooks, handed over or destroyed |
Support and vendor contacts updated | The new named contacts |
Downstream accounts offboarded | Checks in the directories and application consoles |
Open issues and risks transferred | A log with owners |

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
Joiner, mover or leaver workflow starts failing with unauthorised errors | The workflow's owner was disabled or removed, so its token is invalid | Disable the workflow, assign a new owner, enable it. Check the next execution |
A script that used to work returns 401 | The token belonged to the departed person | Issue a token under the service identity and update the script |
Nightly exports or reports stopped arriving | A scheduled search's owner or recipient is gone | Reassign the search and confirm recipients |
Approvals or reviews sit untouched | The approver or reviewer is gone and there is no fallback | Reassign, set a fallback approver and reminders |
Cannot delete an identity | It still owns a source, role, profile or application, or is a reviewer | Reassign those, then retry |
Cannot reset a source | A source owner holds an account on it | Remove that account or change the owner temporarily |

A token stopped working after re-enabling an identity | Disabling disabled the token and re-enabling did not restore it (community report) | Create a new token |
Many tokens stopped on the same day | They shared an expiry date | Renew, and stagger expiry dates |
A form or launcher misbehaves | The owner or an identifier changed | Test it, and recreate or retarget it |
Mail goes nowhere | A personal address in a workflow or template | Move to a shared mailbox |
A returned identity has no admin rights | It was deleted and recreated by aggregation | Re-invite and re-grant levels |

chunks.h: What to do from day one
chunks.x:
Offboarding is cheap if you start the project with the end in mind.
Create workflows, forms and sources under the service identity from the start, not under a personal account that you later have to transfer.
Keep a live owner register from the first sprint.
Use governance groups for ownership of access items.
Prefer shared mailboxes in every template and workflow.
Give every token a purpose, an owner, an expiry and a review date, and stagger expiry dates.
Keep secrets in the vault with two people able to retrieve them.
Write the runbook as if the author were already gone.
Plan the offboarding date at kickoff and put the 90 day inventory in the project plan.

chunks.h: Sources and how far to trust them
chunks.x:
Building a workflow: owner, personal access token, orphaned workflows, reassigning to another administrator, using an account that will not expire. Official.
Working with identities: what disabling and deleting an identity do, and the ownership and reviewer restrictions on deletion. Official.
Managing API keys and personal access tokens: tokens belong to their creator, cannot exceed the owner's access, ten per user, default six month expiry, API clients are not tied to a person. Official. It does not say what happens to a token when its owner is disabled.
Community threads, which are not official: a reply that disabled identities' tokens are disabled too and are not restored on re-enable (PAT behaviour); workflow-owner 401 errors and the owner-switch workaround (workflow owners); reassigning owned objects with workflows or the governance connector (reassign owners, owner termination); and service identities as owners (service accounts).

chunks.h: Sources and how far to trust them
chunks.x: What we could not confirm: what a form does when its owner is removed, whether scheduled searches keep running for a disabled owner, and what happens to a token when its owner is deleted. Test these on a sandbox identity before you rely on an answer.

Produce the owner register now and count objects per implementer.
Name the service identity, its credential and authenticator custodians, and the break-glass holders.
Reassign in the order above, workflow by workflow, with a test after each.
Replace personal tokens and addresses with service-owned, shared ones.
Add the owner-inactive, workflow-failure and token-expiry monitors.

This guide is the document I wished existed on day one of a greenfield SailPoint Identity Security Cloud (ISC, formerly IdentityNow) program. It is written from a real enterprise rollout: a global professional-services firm with roughly 13,000 people, a legacy identity manager being retired, an HR system as the single authoritative source, and a plan to bring well over a hundred applications under governance in two phases.
It is not a tour of the product. SailPoint's own documentation does that. This guide covers what the documentation does not: the decisions you will be forced to make, the places the platform fails silently, the limits you only find by hitting them, and the workaround that finally worked.

chunks.h: SailPoint ISC Greenfield Implementation Field Guide
chunks.x: One model, five processes. Redrawn from the tenant's own overview: everything downstream depends on the HR feed and on the rules that compute the lifecycle state.

chunks.h: Rules that would have saved us weeks
chunks.x:
These are the lessons that cost the most when we learned them late. Each is expanded on its own page.
The HR feed is the product. Every automation downstream is only as good as the authoritative data. Budget real time for data quality, mandatory-field enforcement and an HR change process before you build a single workflow.
Pick one immutable join key and never key on anything else. An employee ID that is never reused, even across rehires, is worth more than any clever correlation rule. Names, emails and login names all change.
Provisioning logic lives in rules, not in source configuration. On a Web Services or JDBC source the endpoint or SQL fields can be empty or dead while a connector rule does all the real work. Review and document rules as first-class deliverables.
The dangerous failures are the quiet ones. A status comparison that stops matching makes every account look enabled. A page-size ceiling silently drops accounts. A swallowed exception sends a request with blank fields. Design monitors for counts and freshness, not just for errors.

chunks.h: Rules that would have saved us weeks
chunks.x:
Set the delete threshold deliberately on every source, and verify it. It is the only thing between an empty API response and a mass account deletion.
Every source needs an aggregation schedule. Two production sources ran for months with none, so reviews and reports showed a stale view that nobody noticed.
Aggregate groups before accounts. Entitlement objects should exist before accounts reference them.
Lifecycle actions target an explicit list of sources. Adding a source later does not add it to your leaver disable action. Make "update the lifecycle state source list" a line in your onboarding checklist.
Forms cannot cascade the way you expect. Dependent dropdowns driven by a search over entitlement attributes do not work. Plan the request experience around this, not against it.
The workflow engine has sharp edges. Secrets can only be created in the UI, an unresolved template path renders as literal text, tier limits count loop bodies, and some approval actions are not licensed. Read the workflow limits before designing a flow.

chunks.h: Rules that would have saved us weeks
chunks.x:
Entitlement value formats are contracts. If a rule parses an identifier out of an entitlement name, changing that format detaches every grant. Treat it like a public API.
Never put credentials, or a debug webhook, in a production rule. Both ended up in ours. One makes provisioning fail whenever a diagnostic listener is down.
Revocation approval is a decision, not a default. Granting needed manager approval while revoking needed none, on thousands of profiles. Decide that on purpose.
Concentrated ownership becomes an outage. Thousands of access profiles owned by one person route every review and escalation through them. Use governance groups.
Automate campaign creation, then verify it. Hundreds of campaigns by hand is not credible. A script that creates them staged and compares them to the source data caught real discrepancies before launch.
Plan notifications and ITSM routing as carefully as provisioning. Most hypercare tickets were about who did or did not receive an email, not about accounts.

chunks.h: Rules that would have saved us weeks
chunks.x:
Switch attribute sync on a couple of attributes at a time. A staged switch-on with validation between steps is the cheapest rollback you will ever get.
Hand over with a documentation pack per integration. Five files per application (reference, tenant context, edge cases, runbook, config evidence) made knowledge transfer routine.

Most pages end with a section titled "What SailPoint's documentation adds". Those sections were checked against SailPoint's public documentation and community in October 2026 and link to their sources.
Observed means it happened on the program. Anything described as a platform limit was measured on a 2026 tenant. SailPoint changes ISC continuously, so re-check a limit before you design around it, especially anything tied to licensing or release level.
Names of internal applications, hosts, accounts, people and identifiers are removed. Commercial products such as Sage People, OneStream, Enate, Dynamics 365 and BMC Helix are named where the integration pattern matters.
Code samples are trimmed and generalised. They show the shape of a solution, not a drop-in implementation.
Dates are expressed as durations. The shape of the timeline matters more than the calendar.

The platform terms you will see throughout: VA is the virtual appliance that sits in your network and talks to your applications. A cluster is a group of VAs. Aggregation is reading accounts or groups from a source into ISC. Correlation is matching an account to an identity. A connector rule runs on the VA around a connector operation; a cloud rule runs inside ISC and has no network access. An entitlement is a single permission on a source, an access profile bundles entitlements for requesting, and a role bundles access profiles or assigns them by criteria.

Joiner, mover and leaver (JML) is the visible face of the program. This page describes how the automation was built from lifecycle states, event-triggered workflows, manager forms and scheduled jobs, and the places where it needed human help.

The HR-driven identity profile had five lifecycle states, all driven by the computed cloudLifecycleState attribute described on the identity model page.
State | Meaning | Account action |
Pre Joiner | Hired, not yet started | Enable the directory accounts |
Active | Employed | Enable the directory accounts |
Intermediate | Anything that fits no other rule | None |
Inactive | Employment ended (end date reached at 22:00 local) | Disable on a list of sources |
Emergency Termination | Manual immediate cut-off | Disable on the directory sources |
Five states. The action attached to each state names its target sources by identifier, so adding a source means adding it to the list.
The lifecycle action source list is explicit
This is the most expensive caveat in this section. Each lifecycle state action names its target sources by ID. At the end of the program the Inactive disable action covered 13 of 146 sources: the directories and the earliest crown-jewel applications. Sources added later were not on the list, including some with no other disable path.

That is not necessarily wrong. Several later applications were handled by compensating mechanisms, for example a scheduled workflow that disables accounts in a payroll SaaS on a half-month calendar, or a manual leaver process. But it has to be a decision, not an accident.
Make this a standing checklist item for every new source:
Is the source account-managed by ISC (it can disable accounts)?
If yes, is it on the Inactive and Emergency Termination action lists?
If no, what disables or reviews access for a leaver, and who owns it?
There is also an organisation setting that controls whether a lifecycle change honours a source's own "can enable" feature flag. It was off. Know its value before you assume lifecycle actions are skipped for sources that cannot enable accounts.
General JML. Redrawn from the design's process figures for joiner, mover and leaver. Movers and leavers take the update branch; the rules engine decides what changes on each target.

chunks.h: The automation layer: events, schedules and forms
chunks.x:
All JML behaviour sat in workflows reacting to platform events. The trigger types used:
Trigger | Fired by | Used for |
Identity attributes changed | A filtered change to one or more attributes | Leaver off-boarding when an end date is set, mover on location change, HR writeback, email-change sync to an app |
Post-provisioning | A completed provisioning plan, filtered by target source and operation (create, enable) | Joiner onboarding and rehire after the directory account exists |
Form submitted | A specific form definition | Manager completes the joiner, mover or leaver form |
Scheduled (cron) | A time | Writeback sweep, a SaaS disable job, the daily leaver job, an "update the identity system" notice |
External HTTP | An authenticated call | A welcome email after account creation in a database application |
Interactive process launched | A launcher in the user portal | Custom access-request forms (see the forms page) |

chunks.h: The automation layer: events, schedules and forms
chunks.x: Filters use JSONPath over the event payload. A leaver trigger watches for cloudLifecycleState changing to inactive; a rehire trigger watches the same attribute going from inactive to active or preJoiner. These filters are exact, so keep the attribute names and values stable.

HR creates the person. The design asked for at least 14 calendar days between request and start date.
The HR source aggregates hourly. ISC creates the identity, computes lifecycle state, login name and email, and moves the lifecycle to preJoiner once the start date is within the processing window.
The lifecycle action enables the directory account. Creation happens in the user's local time zone, 14 days before start.
Directory provisioning sets the identity-derived attributes, places the account in the right organisational unit, adds baseline groups and generates an initial password.
A post-provisioning workflow fires on the committed directory create. It waits (a sleep step) so downstream sync can settle, then:
emails the line manager the credentials and a link to the IT requirements form,
notifies local IT, the HR contact, the finance contact and the central team,
writes the email and login name back to HR (see the identity page).

When the manager submits the form, a form-submitted workflow branches on the answers (for example which applications are needed) and sends mails to the ITSM mailbox that opens tickets. Each branch is a comparison step, so the workflow grows with every application option.
Joiner caveats
Issue | Detail | Mitigation |
No visibility of form completion | ISC could not tell whether the pre-joiner form had been filled in, so it could not re-trigger when the manager changed before the start date | Build a re-send path: an externally triggered workflow or a manually run job. We resent forms by hand dozens of times |
Wrong manager in HR | HR tags the wrong manager when creating the record; the form goes to the wrong person | Fix the data in HR first, then re-send. Do not paper over it in ISC |
Manager does not know the process | Managers on leave, or never told, never complete the form, so the equipment is not released and access is not requested | Communication and training before go-live; reminders; delegate approval |

Duplicate display names | The directory create failed on a duplicate distinguished name or UPN | Unique login names, unique UPN, a retry path (re-provision from ISC after fixing) |
Pre-existing accounts | People who joined before go-live had accounts created by the old tool and needed groups re-pushed | A "new joiner" flag in the identity (hire date compared to today) so legacy cases are handled separately |
Audit evidence | The audit process needed an ITSM ticket per joiner; no manager response meant no ticket | Create the ticket when the form is launched, update it when the form is submitted |

The leaver design had three coordinated parts.
Reminders and the manager form. When an end date is set or changes, a workflow compares it to now and starts a reminder sequence: weekly reminders to the manager until a week before separation, then daily, with the country HR contact copied. The manager completes a leaver form (asset recovery, out-of-office text, who gets the mailbox).
The termination moment. At 22:00 local on the end date the lifecycle becomes inactive. The Inactive action disables the account on the listed sources. The directory disable policy moves the account to a disabled container, hides it from the address list and stamps a note.
Aftercare. A daily scheduled workflow finds leavers by their next-processing date through a search call and loops over them to finish off-boarding. Notifications go to the central team, HR, the finance contact, local IT and the manager.
Leaver caveats

Timing and time zones. Automated tasks run in the user's local time after midnight; the cut-off is 22:00 local on the end date. A last day entered wrongly in HR (or an earlier "IDM disable date" than the stated end date) disables the person early. Several tickets were exactly this.
Group removal is abrupt. On the first day of production the disable removed all groups, including the one that must always remain (the cloud-sync group), cutting a user off from mail who was still active in HR. Fix: keep a list of groups that are never removed, and delay removal of the rest for a number of days after the end date. The design said "seven days after termination only the base groups remain"; build it that way.
Re-adding groups on rehire is not automatic. Previously removed groups do not come back; users must request them again. State this in comms.
Mailbox side effects need a home. Converting the mailbox to shared, setting an out-of-office message, assigning a leaver licence and hiding from the address list were scripted steps in the legacy tool. Inventory them, decide which remain scripts, which become group-driven, and which become workflow steps. Do not assume ISC does them.

Contractors and vendors. Vendor contract expiry arrives as a disable request, not an HR event. Provide an intake and an approval path.
Extended access. HR sometimes asks to extend access after a recorded end date (handover, garden leave). The only clean path is to change the disable date in HR before it passes. Tell HR.

A mover is any change in a mapped attribute, but only some changes need action.
Change | What happens |
Location, region or country | A mover workflow fires, the manager gets a form (asset return, new move date), the directory moves the object to the new container, and the parties are notified |
First or last name | HR changes it; the directory logic generates a new email, UPN and aliases, keeps the old address as an alias, and notifies. Users may need to sign in again because the UPN changed |
Title, department, function | Synced to the directory only if the attribute sync for that attribute is on |
Move to or from a regional delivery centre | Kept as a manual process inherited from the old tool: new account, new mailbox, old account disabled. The user deliberately gets no access to previous mail or profile |
Return from maternity leave to a new role | Not detected as a mover by location logic, so no notification or access change reached local IT. Decide whether role changes should raise a mover form |

Attribute sync is the mover engine
ISC pushes only the attributes you enable in the source's attribute sync configuration. In the directory source about 8 attributes were on and 9 were off (names, display name, phone, employee ID, country code, user type, department were off at the end). This is by design: sync what the application team asked for, nothing else.

Rehire is a lifecycle transition from inactive back to active or preJoiner for an identity that already exists.
The directory account is re-enabled and moved out of the disabled container.
A new initial password is generated and sent to the manager.
Baseline groups return; business groups do not (see above).
The workflow variant for a second directory domain triggers on enable rather than create.
Rehire workflows showed many canceled executions. Investigate cancellations before accepting them as normal; ours were a mix of expected branches and unfinished waits.

Mail was the glue between ISC and everything else. Treat notification design as its own workstream.
Concern | Guidance |
Sender identity | Production mail came from an internal no-reply address; sandbox came from the vendor's default. Tests in sandbox must never go to production distribution lists |
Ticket creation | ISC created ITSM tickets by sending mail to a mailbox with a fixed subject convention. The ITSM side parsed the subject to route to the right queue. Changing the subject breaks routing |
Routing by location | After go-live the subject gained the location so tickets could be assigned to the right local team. Add routing keys early |
Who gets what | Keep a matrix of event by audience (manager, initiator, HR, finance, local IT, central team, ITSM). After go-live the matrix changed: local IT and HR also received the filled form details; central support got a "user account disabled" notice; credentials were restricted to the manager only |

Credentials in mail | Sending credentials to several parties was removed. Send to the manager only, force a reset on first sign-in, and note it in the SOP |
Templates | The tenant ended with about 60 notification templates. Name them by event and audience |
Hypercare showed that most "SailPoint is broken" tickets from regions were notification gaps: a distribution list not updated, a contact wrong in the lookup table, a manager who never received the form, or an ITSM queue not receiving mail. Test every mail path end to end with real recipients before go-live.

For the first weeks of production the team exported a joiner list and a leaver list each night from search (display name, email, created date, lifecycle state, source account count, start or end date, manager) and compared them to HR. Source account count was a cheap health signal: a joiner with fewer accounts than the baseline had a provisioning gap. This took an hour a day and caught problems before users did.

Wait steps and form steps leave many executions in Executing or Canceled. Monitor the count, and know what a normal ratio looks like.
A mover or joiner workflow branching on a dozen application flags becomes unmaintainable. Prefer data-driven branches (a form that lists requested access items) over one comparison step per application.
Do not trigger a workflow from an attribute you also edit for testing. We kept "manual trigger" workflows keyed to a department change; they are a hack and should be disabled once real triggers work.
Put the scheduled catch-up next to every event trigger. Events are lost, and the sweep repairs them.

Enumerate lifecycle states and write down each state's account actions and source list.
Add "update the lifecycle source list" to every source onboarding checklist.
Build the re-send mechanism for forms before go-live.
Define groups that are never removed and delay the removal of the rest.
Inventory legacy mailbox and licensing scripts and assign each a new owner.
Build the notification matrix and test every path end to end.

Most connectivity incidents on the program traced back to the network, not to ISC, and most were resolved by asking the right question of the right team. Work up the stack and stop at the first failure.
Name resolution. Does the host name resolve, to the address you expect, from the VA's network?
Route. Is there a path from the VA to that address?
Port. Does the port accept a connection from the VA?
Transport security. Does the TLS handshake complete, and is the certificate trusted and unexpired?
Authentication. Do the credentials work from the VA?
Application. Does the operation succeed, within the timeout?
Test from the VA itself if you can, because the VA's DNS, route and firewall rules are the ones that count. If the image lacks a tool, test from another host in the same subnet and zone, and say so in your notes.
Work up the stack. Test from the appliance's own network where you can, because its DNS, route and firewall rules are the ones that count.
Commands
Tool availability varies by image, and the VA does not ship a telnet client. Community members report using these on the appliance, with a network utility run inside the appliance's toolbox where it is not on the host. Treat the toolbox detail as community-reported and check your image.

bash
```
# 1. name resolution
nslookup <host>
dig <host>

# 2-3. route and port (use ping only if ICMP is allowed)
nc -vz <host> <port>

# 4. TLS handshake and certificate
openssl s_client -connect <host>:<port> -servername <host>

# 4/6. HTTPS reachability (a HEAD request; connection or TLS errors fail, an HTTP error status does not)
curl -v -I https://<host> --connect-timeout 5

# 6. which containers are up on the VA (community-reported)
docker ps -a
```
A reachability loop over the SailPoint hosts:
bash
```
HOSTS=("<host 1>" "<host 2>" "<host 3>")     # from the current required-URL list
for H in "${HOSTS[@]}"; do
  printf "%-60s " "$H"
  if curl -sS -I "https://$H" --connect-timeout 5 >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo OK; else echo FAIL; fi
done
```

SailPoint has announced that some cloud-hosted endpoints will move to SailPoint-hosted ones. The guidance is to keep the existing entries and add the new ones as they are published. Removing the old ones before the migration finishes is what breaks a VA.

Oracle | 1521 |

Another VA cluster's source | As above, from that cluster |

VA and cluster
Symptom | Likely cause | Check | Resolution |
VA shows Inactive | It cannot reach the service: firewall, proxy, DNS or time | Run the reachability loop from the VA. Check that the other VA is healthy | Get the missing destination allowed. Compare the failing VA's route, proxy and DNS with the healthy one |
Stuck at "update in progress" | An update download was interrupted, or credentials expired after a long outage | Look at container status and the VA logs. Look for download errors or expired credentials | Restore outbound access, avoid repeated restarts during the update, restart the cluster once. If it persists, contact support |
"VA Did Not Update" | The update could not finish | Same as above | Restart the cluster, then support |
Cluster shows "Only 1 VA" | A VA is down or removed | Cluster page | Restore it. A cluster with a disconnected VA receives no updates |
Pairing fails | Code expired (4 hours), passphrase mismatch, no outbound path | Generate a new code. Confirm the same passphrase on each VA | Pair again |

Configuration incomplete | The VA could not connect during setup | Network and time | Fix and wait up to 30 minutes |
Warning for memory or disk | Under-sized VA or debug logging left on | Check sizing and the debug setting | Disable debugging, add resources |
Time drift, odd TLS or token errors | NTP blocked or wrong | timedatectl status | Configure internal NTP on every VA |
Every integration on one cluster fails | The cluster or a shared service account | Cluster status, the shared login | Fix the cluster. This was the first thing to suspect on the program |
One integration fails while its cluster peers are fine | That integration's own route, such as egress or DNS to an external host | Test from the VA to that host | One source reached a vendor host in another geography and was the only one on its cluster that did |
Name resolution
Symptom | Likely cause | Resolution |
Every directory source fails after a DNS change | The VA's DNS servers cannot resolve the domain controllers, or the VA still holds old settings | nslookup the controllers from the VA. Correct the VA's DNS. Reboot the VA (not only the service) so it picks up routes and resolvers |

Works by IP, fails by name | Split-horizon DNS: internal names are not served to the VA's resolver | Point the VA at the internal resolver, or map the host in the VA's hosts file as a stopgap |
Intermittent failures | One of several DNS servers is broken | Query each server directly |
Case-sensitive host lookups in a component | Host name case differs from the application's | Match the case the application uses |
Firewalls and routes
Symptom | Likely cause | Resolution |
"No route to host" | A routing change, a missing route from the VA's subnet, or a firewall rejecting rather than dropping | nc -vz to the host. Ask the network team for the path and the rule hit |
Connection times out | A firewall silently dropping | Same. A timeout points to a drop, a refusal to a closed port |
Connection refused | The service is not listening, or a host firewall | Check the service and the host firewall |
Works from a laptop, not from the VA | The VA's zone has different rules | Test from the VA's subnet |

Works for hours, then fails | Session or idle timeout on a firewall for long-lived or slow connections | Ask for the idle timeout, and keep calls short |
A source in the reserved range | A VA cannot route to 10.255.255.241/28, and a tunnel cannot to 172.16.0.0/22 | Re-address the source or use another method |
Asymmetric routing | Replies take a different path and are dropped | Network team traces both directions |
Proxies and TLS inspection
Symptom | Likely cause | Resolution |
VA cannot reach SailPoint but a browser can | The browser uses a proxy and the VA does not | Configure the proxy on the VA, or open the destinations directly |
TLS errors, "untrusted certificate", S3 download broken | A device inspecting TLS presents its own certificate | Exempt the VA's destinations from inspection, or install the inspection CA on the VA |
Proxy returns 407 | The proxy needs authentication | Use an unauthenticated rule for the VA, or the proxy configuration the VA supports |

A web-services source works in a browser, fails in the connector | A forward proxy sits between the VA and the vendor | Add a bypass for local hosts, or allow the vendor host directly |
Web filter blocks a category | A "new or uncategorised domain" rule | Allow the specific hosts |

Source | Symptom | Likely cause | Resolution |

Active Directory | Works for reads, fails for writes | The directory agent is unreachable or its service account lacks rights | Test the agent port from the VA, check the service and its permissions |
SQL Server | Named instance not found | The browser service port (UDP 1434) is blocked, or the instance has a dynamic port | Use the fixed port in the URL, or allow the browser service |

Databases | TLS or driver errors after a server upgrade | The server requires a newer protocol than the driver offers | Check the driver and server protocol versions |
REST or SaaS | HTTP 429 | A rate limit | Respect the retry header, reduce page size and concurrency |
REST or SaaS | Token endpoint times out under load | The vendor's token service fails under concurrency | Stagger requests |
REST or SaaS | Calls over about a minute fail and later requests from that person are cancelled for an hour | The appliance's call timeout (63 seconds in our measurement) | Keep calls short, split the work, add a timeout in the application |
SFTP | Test connection fails | The URL, the folder permissions, the firewall | See the SFTP page |
Any | Fails only at certain times | A maintenance window, a backup, a batch job at the target | Check the source's schedule against yours |

Symptom | Likely cause | Resolution |

Phase 1 brought in the directory, the HR system and about ten critical applications by hand. Phase 2 had a target of 120 to 135 more applications over five to six quarters, which cannot be done as a series of bespoke projects. This page describes the factory that was set up: how applications were tracked and chased, what the questionnaire asked, the repeatable artefacts for each one, and what the response data taught us about the realistic pace.

A single workbook tracked every application. It had one sheet per phase, a backlog and a response tracker. For the 57 applications in the active list, the columns were:
Group | Columns |
Outreach | initial communication date, reminder, latest response, call scheduled |
Questionnaire | status (received, partial, none) |
People | application owner, technical single point of contact, country, office |
Backlog sheet | status, minutes of meeting, escalated, priority (P1 or P2), call-schedule mail, environment access, region, when the technical contact is available, replaced by |
Keep the owner and the technical contact as separate columns. The business owner answers "who needs access"; the technical contact answers "how is it stored and can we connect". Often they are different people, and about a dozen applications were first "redirected to the technical contact".
The response tracker
From early December to February, about two months of chasing:

Measure | Start | End |
Full responses | 21 | 32 |
Redirected to a technical contact | about 12 | about 15 |
No response | 7 | 0 |
Calls scheduled | | 25 |
Reading it: chasing works, but slowly. No-response fell to zero, yet full responses (32) stayed well below the number of applications in the active list (57), with the rest redirected or scheduled for a call. Plan for a long tail of applications that never answer, and agree in advance what happens to them (retire, defer, or review as a flat file).

About 50 filled questionnaires exist. Each is a short workbook in three sections.
1. Overview
Where it is hosted and who manages it (vendor or in-house).
Whether it has an API for users and groups, and whether the database can be read.
Which environments exist (development, test, production).
2. User management
Who gets access and how it is requested today.
The joiner, mover and leaver process.
Mandatory attributes for an account.
How access is defined (roles, groups, a table) and how changes are made.
How termination is handled.
How often the user list can be synchronised.
The ticket form used, and the team that handles it.
Whether the user list comes from HR or the directory, and whether the directory is mandatory.
Approvals in use.
Access review frequency and criteria.
3. Single point of contact details
Names and contact details for the owner, the technical contact and a deputy.
What the answers looked like

Many answers were "don't know" or a row of question marks. Several applications turned out to be retired or about to be replaced, one payroll product was terminated, and others had no technical owner at all. This is not a failure of the questionnaire. It is the first useful output of the factory: an honest inventory of what is in use and who knows about it. Record the "don't know" answers, since they drive what you do next.
An outreach mail template (initial request, reminder, escalation) was kept with the tracker. Write it once and reuse it for every application.

Every application followed the same document trail:
Artefact | Purpose |
Requirements document | Purpose, application brief (user base, entitlements, environments), current provisioning process, in-scope and out-of-scope operations, demo notes |
Sign-off on requirements | The application owner agrees what will and will not be automated |
Demo | Show the integration working in the sandbox |
Design document | Integration approach, source configuration, schemas, correlation, schedule, provisioning policies, forms, workflows, rules |
System integration test results | Pass or fail per case, with evidence |
User acceptance test | Business sign-off |
Implementation and rollback plan | Ordered steps with a named rollback for each |
End-user manual (SOP) | For the service desk and the approvers |
Documentation pack | The five-file handover (see hypercare page) |
Effort heuristic
The planning heuristic that held up: three to five sessions for requirements, three to five for system integration testing, one to two for production. An integration that needs a custom rule or a database schema takes the upper end or more. Budget the sessions as calendar time with the business, not as build hours; the waiting is what dominates.

Two applications that shared a vendor product but differed in structure became the templates:
A SQL Server application with one database per client. The integration discovers client databases, reads users and groups from each, and provisions into the right one. It needed a multi-database schema document, a JDBC provisioning rule, an access request execution description and a test-evidence document, on top of the usual artefacts.
The single-instance version of the same product. One database, no client dimension. It followed the simple pattern: requirements, an approval process slide, an end-user manual, SIT results, and an implementation and rollback plan.
The multi-database one is the harder case, and its documents are the more detailed. The lesson we would draw (a recommendation, not a measurement) is to pick the hardest representative application first, so its entitlement naming, approval routing, request form and evidence format can be reused by the simpler ones.

Rank the backlog on three axes and make the ranking visible:
Risk. Finance, client data and privileged systems first.
Integration readiness. An application with an API or a readable database ahead of one that needs a project.
Responsiveness. An owner who answers quickly goes before one who does not, because it keeps the factory busy. This is a recommendation, not something the tracker enforced.
Use P1 and P2 rather than a score. Anything that is not P1 or P2 is not in the plan.

ISC is SaaS, but anything it governs inside your network is reached through virtual appliances you run. Most connectivity incidents on the program traced back to a network or cluster decision made in the design phase, so this page is about getting those decisions right.

HR system (authoritative)Hires, moves, leavers, termination dates, manager, location, time zoneWeb Services over REST, hourly
▼
ISC tenant (sandbox + production)Identity profile, transforms, cloud rules, lifecycle states, access model, workflows, forms, campaignsSaaS, outbound-only from your network
▼
HR cluster2 VAs, close to the HR API
Directory clustersOne per forest or region, with IQService for writes
App cluster AREST, SaaS and SQL Server apps
App cluster BFlat-file sources and region-specific apps
▼
TargetsActive Directory, REST applications, SQL databases, SaaS finance and workflow products, an ITSM mailbox

Two tenants: sandbox and production. Build in sandbox, promote to production. They are separate organisations, so credentials, VA registrations and some objects do not travel (see the migration page).
Region is a one-time choice. Both tenants sat in the same cloud region. The VA firewall allow-list needs the region-specific service endpoints (object storage, queue, database, container registry) as well as the US-east defaults, so write the region into the network request.
Org time zone matters. The tenant has an organisation time zone that governs scheduled aggregation times. Workflow schedules carry their own time zone, and identities carry a work-location time zone. That is three time zones in play. Document each one, because a "run at 10pm local" requirement spans all three.

Principles that held up
One cluster per network boundary and blast radius. Group sources by which network they can reach and by how badly you want a fault to spread. We had an HR cluster, a domain cluster per directory estate, an external-directory cluster in another geography, and two general application clusters.
At least two VAs per cluster. VAs update by taking turns, so a single VA means an outage during every update. The design document said two per cluster; the production listing showed the busiest application cluster with one. It also sat in a warning state, and we never proved the cause. Do not run your biggest cluster on one appliance.
Put a cluster near its targets. Latency between a VA and a database shows up as slow or timing-out aggregations. A region-specific app (a platform reachable only from one geography) justified its own placement.
A source cannot simply be moved between clusters. The cluster decides what the source can reach, so choose before you onboard fifty sources onto it.

Clusters fail together. When several unrelated integrations fail at once, suspect the cluster, not the integrations. Write that into your runbook.
Watch cluster status. Two clusters showed a configuring state with an undefined version string for long periods while sources on them still worked. Learn what normal looks like on your tenant so you can spot a real change.
Cluster layout. Redrawn from the design's cluster segregation figure: one cluster for the HR system, one per directory estate (reading directly and writing through a directory agent) and two for applications. The cluster in another geography has a single appliance, a risk the design should have closed.
Sizing and hosting
Decision | Guidance |
VAs per cluster | Minimum two, in different hosts or availability zones |
VM to VA ratio | One to one |
Configuration | Standard (direct outbound). Deep packet inspection is not supported on the path |

Hosting | Public cloud and on-premises hypervisors are both fine, but check the vendor's support list first |
Unsupported hypervisor | We ran some VAs on a hyperconverged stack outside the official support list. SailPoint's answer was that it may work, config is not supported, and they would support the VA once running. Get that in writing before design sign-off |
Network requirements to hand to your network team
The VA only makes outbound calls. Typical requirements:
Requirement | Detail |
Outbound HTTPS 443 to all destinations | Service, update and source traffic |
DNS 53 and NTP 123 | Use an internal NTP server if you block outbound 123, and configure each VA individually |
SSH 22 inbound | Internal only, only if you want to log in to the appliance |
URL allow-list | SailPoint domains, the update service for the appliance OS, feature-flag service, object storage, queue and database endpoints in the US-east region and your region, the container registry in both |

No proxy interference | Web filters and caching products can break the VA. Allow the listed destinations without inspection |
Network methods. The appliance only ever calls out; the one inbound connection is optional administrator SSH. A proxy carries all web traffic while time sync still goes direct. SailPoint advises against the DMZ for security, proximity and connectivity reasons.

Writes to Active Directory (create, move, disable, group changes) go through IQService, a small Windows service. Reads can go direct from the VA. Requirements to plan:
A supported Windows Server with.NET Framework 4.5.2 or later and PowerShell 3.0 or later.
A service account that is a local administrator on the IQService host and an Account Operator or Domain Admin in AD. This is a high-privilege account; scope it as tightly as your model allows and put it under review.
Connectivity from the IQService host to domain controllers on the usual directory ports: LDAP and LDAPS (389, 636), Kerberos (88, 464), AD Web Services (9389), global catalog (3268, 3269), DNS (53), SMB (445) and NetBIOS name and authentication ports.
The Microsoft APIs IQService calls choose their own dynamic ports, so a firewall between the host and the domain controllers must be permissive. Put IQService close to the domain controllers.

Transport security. Ours was configured without TLS to IQService and with plain LDAP to the domain. Decide on TLS from the start; retrofitting it later means touching every domain setting.
Anything that used to be done by scripts in the legacy tool (mailbox conversion, out-of-office, adding licence groups, hiding from the address list) needs an explicit home in the new design. See the Active Directory page.

Pattern | Used for | Notes |
Active Directory connector | Domain accounts and groups | Preferred pattern wherever an application authenticates through AD |
Web Services | HR system, REST applications | All logic in endpoint definitions plus before and after rules |
JDBC | SQL Server applications | Aggregation SQL plus a provisioning rule; there is no provisioning SQL on the source |
Flat file via SFTP (SQL Loader / delimited file) | Applications without an API, and access-review data | Cheap to build and ideal for review-only governance |
Delimited file with no cluster | A tiny admin-identity profile | File upload, no VA needed |
Native SaaS connectors | Dynamics 365, ITSM | Use when the product ships one |
Selection principle used in the design: AD connector first, then a purpose-built direct connector, then JDBC or Web Services, then flat file as fallback. Disconnected (ticket-based) fulfilment is the last resort and should be replaced as soon as a direct integration exists.

Admin automation uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials against the tenant token endpoint, or personal access tokens. Treat both as production secrets (see the security page).
API versions in use were v3, beta and v2025. Newer object families (forms, workflows, launchers) are only on the newest version. Beta endpoints can change shape.
You will script against the API for dumps, bulk changes and campaign creation. Give those scripts their own API client with a documented scope, rather than reusing someone's personal token.

Configure SSO to the production tenant and test it before go-live; the rollout checklist flagged this as a key task.
Create break-glass administrator accounts that do not depend on SSO, and confirm the client's administrators can log in with them.
Keep a Config Hub backup schedule running. The tenant had weekly automated backups plus manual full backups, which made it possible to compare and restore configuration.

Checked against the VA system and network requirements and the tenant connectivity readiness guide in October 2026. Our design matched most of it; these are the details worth adding.
Topic | Documented position |
Minimum VA size | 4 processors, 16 GB memory, 128 GB storage (AWS M5.xlarge, GCP n2-standard-4 or equivalent). The readiness guide quotes a smaller range for local hypervisors and a different Azure size, so trust the requirements page |
Clusters | At least one production cluster and one sandbox cluster, and at least two VAs in each, sandbox included. No load balancer is needed |
Placement | One VA per virtual machine host. Keep a local cluster close to its source system. A DMZ deployment is not recommended |
Updates | Clusters update by rolling, one VA at a time, which is why one VA means an outage |
Network methods | Standard (direct outbound through the firewall, recommended), HTTP proxy, or network tunnel for firewalls that cannot allow domain names. The tunnel is not available in the FedRAMP environment |

Reserved ranges | A source in 10.255.255.241/28 cannot be routed to from any VA. 172.16.0.0/22 is also unusable with the network tunnel |

Geography | VAs cannot be installed in countries with data residency or transmission restrictions, and the page names Russia and China |
Tenant naming | The org name is 3 to 13 characters, and sandbox gets an -sb suffix on its URL |
Administrators | Name break-glass administrators separately for sandbox and production |
