Most of the schedule risk on an ISC program is decided before anyone logs into a tenant. This page covers how to phase the work, what to write down as out of scope, how to run decisions and sign-offs, and the commercial and licensing questions that are easy to leave until they bite.

chunks.h: Phase the program by capability, not by application count
chunks.x:
The program was planned as two phases and that split held up.
Phase | Goal | What was in it |
1 | Prove the platform end to end on the systems that matter most | Authoritative HR source, the main directory domains, about ten crown-jewel applications, joiner and leaver automation, role and criteria-based access, approval-based requests, certification campaigns, standard reports |
2 | Scale to the long tail | An application onboarding factory (see the onboarding page), 120 to 135 more applications, mover automation hardening, segregation-of-duties policies, operations and support service |
A few things worth copying:
Choose phase 1 applications on two criteria together: business criticality and pattern diversity. Criticality decides the shortlist (the systems that hold client, financial or privileged data, where an access review or a fast leaver matters most). Diversity decides the final selection within it, so that you do not spend phase 1 on ten near-identical integrations. Ours covered a directory, an HR system, a REST application, several SQL Server applications and a SaaS finance product. By the end of phase 1 every integration pattern you will use in phase 2 has been exercised once, on systems the business cared about, which also bought the program credibility. Criticality alone gives you ten copies of the same hard problem; diversity alone gives you a showcase nobody needs.

chunks.h: Phase the program by capability, not by application count
chunks.x:
Use cases are incremental. The design document itself noted that no use case is "done" in a single phase. Maturity depends on how many applications and which connector types are live.
Mover is the hard one. It was scoped for phase 2 and still arrived early in a limited form (location, country and region changes), because HR data changes on day one whether you are ready or not. Decide what the platform does on a mover event from the first day of production, even if the answer is "notify and do nothing else".
Two criteria, in order. Criticality builds the shortlist; diversity decides the final selection inside it.

chunks.h: Write out of scope as carefully as in scope
chunks.x:
The approved design listed exclusions explicitly. Each one came back as a question during the program, so having them in writing saved real arguments.
Excluded | What happened later |
Service, functional and bot account governance | A separate service-account governance proposal followed (inventory, ownership, dashboard) once the core platform was stable |
External identities and client-facing systems | Requests arrived for client users on several applications; the answer was "not in this program" and one requirements document recorded it explicitly |
Authentication and single sign-on tooling | Handled by the client's own teams; SSO to the ISC tenant itself still had to be configured and tested |
Privileged credentials | Left with the vault product; one risk entry concerned who stores integration credentials in it |
Password management and sync | Out of scope, which mattered because initial passwords still had to be generated for joiners |

chunks.h: Write out of scope as carefully as in scope
chunks.x:
Custom connector development, UI customisation, code-level branding | Only out-of-the-box connectors and features; everything custom is a rule, workflow or form |
Data cleansing, migration and reconciliation | The client owns data fixes, but the program still had to quantify the problem (see the identity model page) |
User acceptance test management | The client runs UAT; the integrator supports it |
Non-functional testing | Not performed |
Custom reports | Only out-of-the-box reports and search exports |
Sandbox and UAT identities | No governance of non-production identities |
For each exclusion, also write down the intake route. "Out of scope" is not an answer for the requester; "raise it here and it goes to the backlog" is.

chunks.h: Decide the approach: lift and shift or redesign
chunks.x:
The client's existing process for several applications was ticket-driven: a manager raised an ITSM ticket and an application team provisioned manually. For some applications the program deliberately lifted and shifted that process, keeping the ITSM ticket as the trigger and using ISC only to execute the access.
That is a legitimate choice, but it moves risk rather than removing it:
Two approvals existed (the ITSM ticket and the ISC request). By agreement the ISC approval was removed for one application. Because the request center is visible to the whole company, the risk register recorded that an illegitimate user could in principle request elevated access. The mitigation has to be designed, for example by making the request entry point a launcher form visible only to the operations team (see the forms page).
Lift and shift keeps the human bottleneck. It is fine for phase 1 and should be a conscious backlog item to remove later.

chunks.h: Decide the approach: lift and shift or redesign
chunks.x: Record the decision, the residual risk and the mitigation in the RAID log at the time you make it.

Mechanism | Use |
Weekly delivery follow-up | Tasks, blockers, next steps per application |
Monthly high-level status | Progress, change requests, decisions needed |
RACI | Who is responsible, accountable, consulted, informed, per deliverable |
Decision matrix (PACE style) | Who proposes, approves, consults and executes a decision, so decisions do not stall |
RAID log | Risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies. Reused as the hypercare issue log |
Technical design authority review | A gate on the design before build |
Change advisory board per application | Opened ahead of cutover, one change record per application |
Practical notes:
Stakeholder register early. Business owner, technical owner, infrastructure contact and functional contact are four different people per application. Missing any of them stalls onboarding.
Sign-off discipline. Every application had a requirements document that needed sign-off, then a demo, then a design document. Sign-off threads needed repeated chasing and "urgent approval required" subject lines. Put a sign-off deadline in the plan and name a deputy who may sign.

Scope changes belong in the document. When a stakeholder said client-user provisioning was not in scope, the requirement document was updated in the same thread. That sentence prevented a later dispute.
Keep the integrator out of UAT ownership. The go-live checklist itself said the person who runs the pre-UAT check should not be the implementer.

Role | Notes |
Sponsor and accountable owner | Removes organisational blockers |
Project manager | Plan, RAID, comms, change records |
Solution architect | Owns the design document and pattern choices |
ISC engineers | Source, rule, workflow and form build |
Directory and mail specialist | AD, Exchange and licensing side effects of lifecycle events |
HR system owner | Data quality, new fields, the termination date process |
Application owners and technical SPOCs | Requirements, lower environments, test, sign-off |
ITSM owner | Queues, mailboxes and templates that ISC mails into |
Security and risk | Reviews secrets handling, access model, campaign design |
Local IT contacts per country | Receive joiner and leaver notifications; need data upkeep |

chunks.h: Assumptions to write down on day one
chunks.x:
Every one of these became a real problem when left implicit:
Lower environments exist for each in-scope application and the integrator can reach them.
A service account with sufficient but not excessive rights can be created for ISC on each target.
Network paths from the VA clusters to every target are open, including ports and DNS.
HR can change its process (mandatory fields, termination date handling, rehire rule) and will.
Application owners are the right people to approve access, and they know it.
Notification mailboxes, ITSM assignment queues and distribution lists are created before testing, not during.
Joiner lead time is long enough (the design used 14 days before start) for managers to act.
Vendors of SaaS applications will expose APIs for user management, or the fall-back is a flat file.

Identity count versus licensed users. The authoritative feed brought in about 43,000 identities for a workforce of roughly 13,000 because historical leavers lived in the HR system. Ask SailPoint exactly how identities are counted for licensing, and decide whether to filter old leavers in the HR query rather than carry them forever. Both the identity profile count and the licensed registered-user cap are in the tenant API, and they were far apart.
Product modules. Confirm which modules are licensed before designing around them. In our tenant the generic approval workflow action was not licensed (it saved but failed to enable), segregation of duties policies were empty, and several admin APIs returned not-available responses. Treat unlicensed capabilities as out of scope in the design rather than discovering them during build.
Sandbox is not production. Plan for the sandbox tenant to be used for build and the production tenant for operations only. Identities in the sandbox are out of scope for governance.

For a JDBC application with a clear schema the integration team used this shape, which turned out to be realistic:
Stage | Effort shape |
Requirement gathering | 3 to 5 working sessions, plus access and DB connection details up front |
Build and configuration | Integrator-led, light dependency on the application team |
System integration testing | 3 to 5 sessions to validate data |
User acceptance testing and sign-off | Client-led, with test results shared for sign-off |
Production deployment | 1 to 2 sessions, repeating the same steps as lower environments |
REST integrations with token handling, pagination or custom endpoints are heavier; budget the first of each pattern at several times the repeat cost.

chunks.h: How this compares with SailPoint's own phased path
chunks.x:
SailPoint publishes a phased approach to identity security that is a useful sanity check on any plan. Checked against our program in October 2026:
SailPoint's phase | Their guidance | What we did |
1. Foundational governance | Connect the authoritative HR system, model identities, connect core directories, verify and correct data before relying on it, run targeted certifications | Same order. The data correction step was where we under-planned (see the identity model and go-live pages) |
2. Expansion and lifecycle | Contractors and other non-employees next, then critical applications, then joiner, mover, leaver automation | We folded joiner and leaver into phase 1 and left movers for phase 2. Contractors were part of the HR feed; we did not evaluate a separate non-employee product |
3. Activity and machines | Activity data, machine and service-account discovery | Out of scope. Service accounts became a separate governance proposal |

chunks.h: How this compares with SailPoint's own phased path
chunks.x:
4. Access modelling and requests | Role-based access, request workflows, service desk and collaboration integrations | Overlapped phase 1 and 2 |
5. Cloud, data and privileged | Cloud infrastructure entitlements, data access, privileged integration | Out of scope by design |
6. Maturity | On-premises servers and databases, separation of duties, periodic strategy review | Separation of duties was a phase 2 item |
Two things to take from the comparison. First, SailPoint's own advice agrees that data verification precedes certifications, which matches our experience. Second, it names contractors and non-employees as an explicit early step. If your workforce includes many, decide on day one whether they come through the HR feed, a non-employee lifecycle product or a flat file.
The six phases. Structure follows SailPoint's published phased approach; the tags show where the program sat against it.

Prioritisation criteria from SailPoint
The connectivity workstream guidance says to evaluate each application on three things: its priority to the business, its impact (how critical it is to operations and how much access control it holds) and its readiness for integration. It also advises integrating directories and single sign-on first, then applications in manageable phases, and it warns that unknown ownership and missing information are the main reasons onboarding stalls. A practical scoring sheet, combining the three criteria with ours:
Criterion | Question | Weight it when... |

Business criticality | Would an access failure here hurt revenue, clients or compliance? | Always. It sets the shortlist |

Create the stakeholder register with four contacts per application.

An identity platform holds the keys to everything else, so its own hygiene matters more than most systems. This page lists what we found when we audited the tenant after build, the habits that would have prevented each finding, and how to handle the sensitive material a project like this generates. Everything here is generalised; none of it names the client.

Finding | Where | Why it matters |
A hard-coded Authorization: Basic header | Two operations on one Web Services source | The credential lives in the source definition and is returned by the source API to anyone who can read it |
An OAuth client_secret and a password grant in plaintext HTTP bodies | Two HR writeback workflows, while other workflows used $.secrets.* | Workflow definitions are readable and exportable, so the secret travels with them |
A client id stored in clear text | A REST source. It was not on the encrypted list, and GET /sources/{id} returns it | Half of a credential pair is still a credential |
A service credential embedded as URL query parameters | Two connector rules. GET /connector-rules/{id} returns the script in clear text | The credential is in the rule body, in logs, and in any proxy that records URLs |
A debug webhook helper | Four production rules | Sends rule data to an external listener. Provisioning fails whenever the listener is down |

A predictable initial password | The directory create policy, built from slices of HR attributes | Anyone who knows an employee's record can compute it |
14 OAuth clients and 10 personal access tokens | Tenant-wide | None had a documented owner or rotation date |
None of these were exotic. Each was a shortcut taken during build, in a sandbox, that was promoted unchanged.

Secrets
Credentials belong in the platform's secret store or in the source's encrypted attributes, never in a rule, a workflow body, an HTTP header field or a query string.
Know what your read APIs return. The source, connector-rule and workflow APIs return their definitions. Anything not marked encrypted is visible to every administrator and every token that can read them.
Use per-environment credentials. The sandbox and production integrations should not share a service account. Config Hub does not carry source secrets across tenants, so expect to re-enter them in production (see the go-live page); use that moment to issue new ones.
Never pass credentials as URL parameters. Move them to a header or a body, supplied from a secret.
Prefer the secret reference over a pasted value in workflows. Secrets can only be created in the UI, which is a nuisance, but it is the only safe route. Plan for it in the deployment checklist.

Rotate when in doubt. A credential pasted into a chat, a ticket or a shared document is exposed. Rotate it in the source and in every rule or workflow that repeats it. Find the repeats with a search over exported configuration before you rotate, not after.
Rules and debugging
If a rule needs diagnostics, log through the platform's logging, not through an external webhook.
If you must keep a debug helper, gate it behind a flag that defaults to false and make the helper swallow its own failures so a dead listener cannot break provisioning. Review every production rule for the flag's value as part of go-live.
Inventory connector rules and cloud rules as code. Cloud rules cannot be read with GET; export them through the configuration export with type RULE.
Changes to some rules may need SailPoint to deploy them. Allow for that in release planning.
Passwords
Generate initial passwords from a random source, not from attributes. If the first-login flow is the only use, expire it.

Deliver credentials to the right person. A recurring hypercare ticket was a credentials mail reaching the wrong recipient after a manager change.
Tokens and clients
Practice | Why |
Inventory every OAuth client and PAT with an owner and purpose | Unowned credentials are never rotated |
One client per integration, with the least scope that works | A leak is then bounded |
Set an expiry or a review date | Stale tokens outlive the people who made them |
Do not share one administrator token across scripts and people | There is no audit trail otherwise |
Rotate on staff departure | A PAT is tied to its creator's rights |

A tenant dump, an exported configuration and a set of troubleshooting notes are all sensitive data. We took a full JSON dump of the tenant to support analysis, and it contained source configuration, rules, workflow definitions and, where an attribute was not marked encrypted, credentials.
Store dumps in access-controlled locations and delete them when the analysis is done.
Do not email them. Do not paste them into a chat or a ticket.
Redact before sharing. Replace anything credential-shaped. Strip query-string credentials and long hex literals. A helper that replaces values for named keys and masks long random strings catches most of it.
Keep a clean redacted copy of each integration's configuration with its documentation pack. It is the evidence that the handover is complete, without being a liability.

The encrypted list on a source is data, and it can drift. We found duplicates and entries added by hand. A key that should be encrypted but is not on the list is stored and returned in clear.
The features list can overstate capability. A source that declares it can create and enable accounts does not mean those operations are wired up. Check by running one, then record the real capability statement in the documentation.
Test and copy objects accumulate. Workflows and forms created for tests were left in place. Delete them or mark them clearly; each one is a potential path for a mistake.
Do not leave the delete threshold at a permissive value. See the connectors page; it is a security control as much as a safety one.

The program deliberately excluded:
Privileged credentials, which stay in a vault and are not managed by ISC.
Service accounts. Their governance was recorded as a separate proposal rather than stretched into the HR-driven lifecycle. The proposal was an inventory database fed by the vault, the directory and an ISC extract, with a reporting layer on top, delivered in phases. The database was recommended over a direct dashboard connection because it keeps correlation, history and resilience, and avoids exposing credentials to the reporting tool.
State your exclusions in the scope document. An auditor will ask where service accounts and break-glass access are governed, and "later, here is the plan" is a better answer than silence.

Create break-glass administrators in each tenant before go-live, store their credentials in the vault, and test them.
Keep the number of full administrators small. The tenant held 14 clients and 10 tokens; the same discipline applies to people.
Record who can edit rules, workflows and sources. Treat the ability to change a connector rule as the ability to read or change anything that source touches.

chunks.h: A short security review you can run in a day
chunks.x:
List every source and check which attributes are on the encrypted list against the attributes that look like secrets.
Search exported rules, workflows and forms for Authorization, password, secret, token, client_secret and for URLs with ? and =.
Read the 5 most privileged rules end to end.
Inventory OAuth clients and PATs, with owner and last use.
Check that every enabled workflow's secrets are references.
Check initial password generation.
Confirm the delete threshold of every source.
Look for debug helpers and test objects.

Ban credentials in rules, workflow bodies and URLs from the first build. Review for it at every promotion.
Inventory OAuth clients and tokens with owners, and rotate them on a schedule.
Treat tenant dumps and exports as sensitive; redact before sharing; delete when finished.
Rotate any credential that has been pasted anywhere it should not have been.
Write the scope exclusions (privileged accounts, service accounts) down with the plan for them.
Run the one-day security review before go-live and again at the end of hypercare.

About 120 of the 146 sources on the program were flat files, so the SFTP server behind them was one of the most important pieces of infrastructure in the estate. This page describes the design we used, a build recipe for a Linux SFTP host, the source configuration that reads from it, the file hygiene that keeps reviews correct, and what goes wrong. The commands are examples for a Linux host with OpenSSH. Adapt them to your standards and have your platform team review them.

chunks.h: How a flat-file source reaches the file
chunks.x:
On the program the flat-file sources were SQL Loader sources, not the delimited-file type. A SQL Loader source reads a CSV file through a text-file database driver and queries it with SQL, so each file is a table. The virtual appliance opens an SFTP connection to the file server, reads the file and aggregates it like any other source.
text
```
Application owner  ->  CSV file  ->  SFTP server  <-- SFTP (22) --  Virtual appliance cluster  ->  ISC source
                                      (one folder and one login per application)
```
The delimited-file source type is the alternative. It is loaded by uploading the file through the UI or API, with no appliance and no server, and it suits small, manual loads. The program used SQL Loader, so that a tool could drop a file and ISC could read it on a schedule. If you need neither a schedule nor an appliance, upload is simpler.
Flat-file path. One shared host, one login and folder per application. Only the appliances and the placement tool connect; application owners never do.

What we observed on the program: one shared Linux SFTP host, one login and one folder per application, the login and an encrypted password stored in the source, and files placed by an administrator tool that used elevated rights on the server. The chroot, the source-address restriction and the scripts on this page are our recommended hardening, not a description of what the program had.
Decision | What we did | Why |
One server, shared | A single Linux SFTP host reachable from the appliance cluster that serves flat files | Cheap, central, one place to monitor |
One folder and one login per application | Each source has its own SFTP user and folder | One application's credentials cannot read another's file |
One file per source and cycle | A new, clearly named file for each review cycle | The history is explicit and a reviewer's file is never overwritten |
File name equals table name | The SQL in the source selects from a table named like the file (without the extension) | The driver treats each file in the folder as a table |

Password authentication, source credentials in the source | The source stores the SFTP user and an encrypted password | That is how the source authenticates. Restrict by source address (recommended) |
Admin access by a named administrator with elevated rights | Files are put in place by an automated tool or an administrator, not by application owners | Application owners email a file, a controlled process places it |
Placement | Reachable by the cluster that serves the source, on a network the appliances can route to | The appliance, not ISC, connects |
Several of these are choices, not rules. A cloud object store with SFTP access, a managed file transfer product, or an existing corporate SFTP service may suit you better, as long as the appliance can reach it and it supports the connection the driver needs. Confirm with a test before you commit.

1. Prepare the host
A hardened Linux host with time synchronised to your internal time source.
A separate data volume for the SFTP area, monitored for free space.
Backups of the data area on your normal schedule (the files are evidence for reviews).
OpenSSH server, a host firewall, and a log shipper to your central logging.
2. Create the group and the base directory
bash
```
# one group for every application login
sudo groupadd sftp-apps

# base directory owned by root (required if you use a chroot)
sudo mkdir -p /srv/sftp
sudo chown root:root /srv/sftp
sudo chmod 755 /srv/sftp
```
3. Create an application login and folder
Repeat for every application. Use a script (below) so the settings are identical every time.
bash
```
APP=app01                               # lower case, no spaces
sudo useradd -g sftp-apps -s /usr/sbin/nologin -d /srv/sftp/$APP -M $APP
# set a long random password and store it in your vault, not in a ticket
sudo passwd $APP

# chroot directory: must be owned by root and not writable by anyone else
sudo mkdir -p /srv/sftp/$APP/data
sudo chown root:root /srv/sftp/$APP
sudo chmod 755       /srv/sftp/$APP

# writable folder inside the chroot
sudo chown $APP:sftp-apps /srv/sftp/$APP/data
sudo chmod 750            /srv/sftp/$APP/data
```

4. Configure OpenSSH for SFTP only
Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config (or a file in sshd_config.d):
text
```
Subsystem sftp internal-sftp

Match Group sftp-apps
    ChrootDirectory /srv/sftp/%u
    ForceCommand internal-sftp
    PasswordAuthentication yes
    PermitTTY no
    AllowTcpForwarding no
    X11Forwarding no
    AllowAgentForwarding no
```
Optionally restrict logins to the appliance addresses:
text
```
Match Group sftp-apps Address <VA 1 address>,<VA 2 address>
    ChrootDirectory /srv/sftp/%u
    ForceCommand internal-sftp
```
(Combine the conditions on a single Match line, and keep your administrators in a different group that is not forced into internal-sftp.) Test the configuration, then reload:
bash
```
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
```
5. Firewall
From | To | Port | Purpose |
Appliances in the cluster | SFTP host | 22 | The source reads the file |
Administration host | SFTP host | 22 | Placing files, maintenance |

Nothing else | | | Application owners do not connect |
6. Test before you wire a source
bash
```
# from a host in the same network zone as the appliances
sftp app01@<sftp host>
sftp> ls
sftp> put test.csv data/test.csv
sftp> bye
```
Then run Test Connection from the ISC source, which is the test that matters, because it uses the appliance's network path and the driver's own client.
A reusable onboarding script
bash
```
#!/bin/bash
# add_app.sh <name>  - creates a login and folder for one application
set -euo pipefail
APP="$1"
[[ "$APP" =~ ^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{2,30}$ ]] || { echo "bad name"; exit 1; }
id "$APP" &>/dev/null && { echo "exists"; exit 1; }

useradd -g sftp-apps -s /usr/sbin/nologin -d /srv/sftp/$APP -M "$APP"
mkdir -p /srv/sftp/$APP/data
chown root:root /srv/sftp/$APP && chmod 755 /srv/sftp/$APP
chown "$APP":sftp-apps /srv/sftp/$APP/data && chmod 750 /srv/sftp/$APP/data

PW=$(openssl rand -base64 24)
echo "$APP:$PW" | chpasswd
echo "Created $APP. Store this password in the vault now: $PW"
```

The source attributes that mattered on the program (values are placeholders):
json
```
{
  "type": "SQLLoader",
  "connectorAttributes": {
    "driverClass": "com.hxtt.sql.text.TextDriver",
    "url": "jdbc:csv:/sftp://<sftp host>/<folder>/",
    "user": "<application login>",
    "password": "<set in the UI, encrypted>",
    "additionalConnProperties": ["_CSV_Header=true", "lockTimeout=30000"],
    "SQL": "select * from <file name without extension> order by [<id column>]",
    "testConnSQL": "select * from <file name without extension> order by [<id column>]",
    "indexColumns": ["<id column>"],
    "mergeRows": true,
    "mergeColumns": ["<entitlement column>"],
    "disableOrderingCheck": true,
    "deleteThresholdPercentage": 10,
…
```
Setting | Meaning and advice |
url | The data-files URL. The format is jdbc:csv: followed by /sftp://host/folder/. The documentation shows a variant without the leading slash, so test which one your server needs. Use a path the SFTP login can reach from its starting directory |

user, password | The application login. Set the password in the UI so it is stored encrypted |
_CSV_Header=true | The first row is the column header |
lockTimeout=30000 | SailPoint recommends at least 30000 ms for remote connections. Without it, a default of one second caused "timeout beyond 1000 ms to open a table" |
SQL | Reads the file as a table. The table is the file name without the extension |
indexColumns, mergeRows, mergeColumns | When several rows describe one account (one row per entitlement), merge them into one account with a multi-valued attribute. These are not in the UI. Add them with the API. The query must be ordered by the index column |
disableOrderingCheck | Skips the sorted-input check. Only safe if you sort the file yourself |
deleteThresholdPercentage | Set it. A truncated or empty file is the commonest cause of mass removal on a flat-file source |
Add the merge attributes with a JSON patch (confirm the path syntax for your API version):

json
```
[
  { "op": "add", "path": "/connectorAttributes/mergeRows", "value": true },
  { "op": "add", "path": "/connectorAttributes/mergeColumns", "value": ["<entitlement column>"] },
  { "op": "add", "path": "/connectorAttributes/indexColumns", "value": ["<id column>"] }
]
```
Schema and correlation
Define the account schema from the column names, and mark the identifier, display name and entitlement attributes.
Correlate on one attribute (the email address or the login name), chosen by match rate against the identity cube.
Run an account aggregation and review the uncorrelated list before you build campaigns on the source.

Most flat-file failures are file problems. Apply these to every file before it is placed:
Rule | Why |
UTF-8 encoding | Special characters otherwise appear corrupted after aggregation |
A header row that matches the schema | A new column that is not in the SQL is ignored |
Sorted by the index column when merging | The driver fails with "data should be sorted in ascending order", or accounts split |
One spelling of every id | USER01 and user01 in one file made ISC drop one spelling |
No stray apostrophes or spaces in headers | Header names become column names |
Consistent line endings | CRLF is safe |
Atomic placement | Upload under a temporary name and rename, so the appliance never reads a half-written file |
Never overwrite a different file of the same name | Place the new one with a suffix and reconcile |
Record a checksum | Prove later which file a campaign was built from |
A small preparation script that fixes the common problems:

python
```
import csv, sys

src, dst, id_col = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]

with open(src, newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

if not rows:
    sys.exit("refusing to write an empty file")

for r in rows:
    for k in r:
        r[k] = (r[k] or "").strip()
    r[id_col] = r[id_col].lower()          # one spelling of every id

rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[id_col])

with open(dst, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0].keys()), lineterminator="\r\n")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)

print("wrote", len(rows), "rows")
```
Placing a file as an administrator
On the program, an automated tool placed the files through a staging folder, with elevated rights on the server. The pattern is worth copying even if your tool is a shell script:
Upload to a staging folder the administrator owns.
Use sudo install -o <app login> -g <group> -m 664 <staged> <target> to put the file where the application login can read it, with the right owner.

If a file of that name already exists and its checksum differs, place the new one under a different name and stop.
Remove the staged copy.
Read the file back and compare the checksum before aggregating.

Check | Why |
Free space on the data volume | A full disk makes uploads fail |
Age of the newest file per application | Stale files produce stale reviews. Compare with the aggregation schedule |
Count of lines per file against the last | A sudden drop is a truncated file |
Failed login attempts | Brute force against password logins |
Connection count from unknown addresses | Anyone other than the appliances and administrators |
Source health in ISC | The first signal that the file or the path is wrong |
Backup success | The files are the evidence for reviews |
Housekeeping:
Keep files for the retention period your audit requires, then archive.
Rotate application passwords on a schedule and when staff leave, and update the source when you do.
Review the list of logins quarterly against the list of live sources.
Treat the server as a controlled system: patched, logged, and covered by your normal access review.

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
Test Connection: "verify that the location in the Data Files URL is correct" | The URL format or the path is wrong | Use jdbc:csv:/sftp://host/folder/, and the complete path for the default folder. Check with a manual SFTP session |
"timeout beyond 1000 ms to open a table" | The lock timeout is too short for a remote file | lockTimeout=30000 as an additional connection parameter |
"Failed to load table...: read-only file system" | The login cannot write where the driver needs to | Check permissions on the folder |
"Driver is not valid" with a text file | The file is a text file, not CSV | Use the text variant of the URL and the matching extension property |
"Data should be sorted in ascending order" | Merging is on and the file is not sorted | Sort the file, or add an order by to the query |
One entitlement per account | Rows for one account are not adjacent | Sort by account id |

Special characters appear as symbols | Wrong encoding | Save as UTF-8 and re-run |
A new column is not picked up | The SQL lists columns | Add the column to the query |
A disabled account is removed after a maintenance task | The source cannot re-read a provisioned account | Add the get-object query |
Aggregation fails after a credential change | A cached pooled connection | Disable pooling through the API, as documented for the connector |
Intermittent timeouts or "login failed" | The documentation warns SFTP can fail intermittently for this connector | Retry, check server load and connection limits, and keep files small |
The source reads an old file | A different file of the same name was not replaced | Check names and checksums, and the folder the URL points to |
Everything fails at once | The server, the firewall or DNS | Test from a host on the appliance's network |

Passwords for application logins are credentials. Store them in a vault, never in a spreadsheet or a ticket.
The file contains personal data about people and their access. Restrict who can read the folders, encrypt backups, and delete files when retention ends.
Do not let the server initiate connections to the internet.
A flat-file source is only as accurate as the file. Record who produced it and when.
Where the file is built from another system, automate it. A manual export that someone forgets to run is the commonest cause of a stale review.

Decide on SQL Loader, upload, or an existing transfer service for each application before you build the server.
Build one login and one folder per application, from a script.
Put the file hygiene rules in a script that every file passes through.
Set the delete threshold, the lock timeout and the merge attributes on every source.
Monitor file age and size as well as source health.
Keep a record of which file each campaign was built from.

Every on-premises source in the program reached ISC through a virtual appliance (VA) in a cluster. This page is the build procedure, in the order we would do it again: plan the clusters, prepare the network, deploy the image, pair it with the tenant, verify, and then operate it. It follows SailPoint's published procedure (checked against the VA documentation in October 2026) and adds the planning and checks that the documentation leaves out. Commands are from the documentation unless marked otherwise. Re-check them against the current VA guide before use, because images and tooling change.

Decide this before you deploy anything. Sources are attached to a cluster, and moving fifty sources later is painful.
Question | Guidance |
How many clusters? | At least one for production and one for sandbox. Add clusters per network boundary and per blast radius |
How many VAs per cluster? | At least two, sandbox included. Updates roll through one VA at a time, so one VA means an outage on every update |
Where do VAs sit? | Close to the sources they serve. One VA per virtual machine host, spread across hosts or availability zones. SailPoint advises against the DMZ |
Which sources on which cluster? | Group by reachability and risk. The program used a cluster for HR, one per directory estate, one for application sources and one for flat files and region-specific systems, 5 clusters and 9 appliances in all |
What is the network method? | Standard (direct outbound), HTTP proxy, or network tunnel. Pick one per cluster and keep each cluster consistent |

Time zone | Set per cluster. It governs aggregation schedules and does not shift for daylight saving |
Cluster type | Standard, unless you also run the product that needs the harvester type. The type cannot be changed afterwards |
Write the plan as a table and keep it with the architecture document:
Cluster | Purpose | Sources | VAs | Host or zone | Network method | Owner |
<env>-<purpose> | | | 2 | | Standard | |
Order matters. The network and the plan come first; sources are attached only after every appliance shows connected and a failover test has passed.

Item | Requirement (per VA) |
Compute | 4 processors, 16 GB memory, 128 GB storage as a minimum image. Cloud equivalents: a 4 vCPU general-purpose instance |
Processor | A supported Intel or AMD generation exposed by the hypervisor |
Hypervisor | vSphere 8.0 or later, Hyper-V Server 2016 or later, or a supported cloud |
Network | Outbound 443 to SailPoint and the listed services, DNS (53), NTP (123), and the ports of the sources it serves |
Time | Synchronised. Internal NTP if outbound 123 is closed |
DNS | Reaches your internal DNS servers, so it can resolve source host names |
Optional components | A Privileged Access Gateway or Data Access Security collector adds processors and memory |
Restrictions | No third-party monitoring agents. Not in restricted geographies. Not in 10.255.255.241/28, which a VA cannot route to |
Write these down for the network team before the build (see the network page for a firewall request template).

chunks.h: Step 2: obtain and deploy the image
chunks.x:
Platform | How |
vSphere | Download the package from the VA documentation page and deploy it with your standard process |
Hyper-V | Use the package labelled for Azure, which contains a sailpoint-va.vhd. Create a Generation 1 VM, give it the memory the requirements page states, connect it to an external virtual switch and attach the existing disk |
AWS | Open a support request for an image (AMI) identifier, giving your account number and region. Launch it with an instance size that meets the requirements, enable instance metadata access with a hop limit of 2, and use a security group that allows port 22 from your range |
Azure | The extracted disk is about 132 GB. Upload it to a storage container, create a managed disk from it, then create the VM from that disk (Linux, a size that meets the requirements) with a network security group that allows port 22 |
Google Cloud | Extract the image, upload it to a storage bucket, import it as a custom image without OS adaptation, and create an instance with a 128 GB boot disk |

chunks.h: Step 2: obtain and deploy the image
chunks.x:
For every platform: start the VM, then sign in to the console or over SSH as the sailpoint user with the default password given in the documentation, and change it immediately:
bash
```
passwd
```
Store the new password in your vault. If it is lost, a new VA has to be created. On a cloud VM, if a failed DHCP-related service is reported after login, the documentation says to disable it:
bash
```
sudo systemctl disable esx_dhcp_bump.service
```
On Hyper-V, disable the Azure agent to prevent DNS and routing problems:
bash
```
systemctl status waagent
sudo systemctl mask waagent
sudo reboot
```

sudoedit /etc/systemd/network/static.network

[Network]
DNS=<dns server>

Local NTP
Where outbound NTP is closed, point each VA to your internal server. Each VA is configured separately:
bash
```
sudoedit /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf        # set NTP=<server names or addresses>, uncomment it
sudo systemctl restart systemd-timesyncd
timedatectl status
```
Host name mappings for sources
If a source host name does not resolve through DNS, map it in /home/sailpoint/hosts.yaml and restart the service. Indentation is exact: two spaces before the address, four spaces then a dash before each name.

chunks.x:

```
hosts:
  10.20.30.40:
    - host1.domain.example
    - host1
```

```

```

HTTP proxy
Copy the proxy template from SailPoint's community into /home/sailpoint/ and set it:
yaml
```

http_proxy: http://<proxy>:<port>/

For firewalls that can allow IP addresses but not domain names. It needs outbound 443 to the regional tunnel addresses. The setup guide is on SailPoint's community, behind a login, and the tunnel is not available in some government environments.

va-bootstrap set-passphrase
va-bootstrap pair

va-bootstrap pair             --http-proxy <http://host:port> --https-proxy <http://host:port>
```

In the cluster, Edit, Virtual Appliances, Add New, VA.
Enter the pairing code shown on the VA in the configuration page, and select Pair.

Rule | Detail |
Passphrase | The same on every VA in the cluster. It cannot start with a special character or contain !, /, \ or spaces |
Pairing code | Valid for 4 hours. Generate a new one if it expires |
Association | By passphrase and pairing code, not by a key file |

chunks.x:

Port reachability | The source port answers from the VA |

Take a VM snapshot after a good configuration, as SailPoint suggests, and delete it once the VA has joined its cluster.

Select the cluster on the source. If the source supports TLS, enable it, and the certificate is copied to the cluster.
Run Test Connection, then a first aggregation, then a full run.
Record the source, cluster and owner in the cluster plan.
For directory sources that write, install and test the directory agent on the Windows host (see the directory page).

Task | How |
Health | Cluster and VA badges in the tenant, plus the monitors from the hypercare page |
Restart the cluster | Menu, Restart, confirm. This is the usual first step for a stuck or non-updating VA |
Updates | Rolling, one VA at a time, not skippable, with no notice. A cluster with a disconnected VA receives no updates at all, so fix an inactive VA quickly |

Containers restarting repeatedly | If a container restarts more than 10 times in 30 minutes, update and restart the cluster |
Password | passwd as sailpoint, then sudo reboot. Save it |

Adding a VA to a cluster
Deploy the image, apply the network settings, run va-bootstrap set-passphrase with the cluster's passphrase and va-bootstrap pair, and add it in the cluster. Keep two or more in every cluster.
Replacing or retiring a VA
Delete a VA from the cluster's edit page, then shut down the instance on your platform. A VA cannot be deleted if it is the only one in its cluster and still has a source attached.
SailPoint advises against moving or migrating existing VAs. Replace by building new.
A failed cluster is replaced by creating a new cluster with at least two VAs, pointing each source at it, checking the connections, and then deleting the old cluster. Expect to re-enter source credentials when a source moves to a different cluster.

The documented approach is a second cluster, not a standby VA: a new cluster is built, sources are re-pointed, and credentials are re-entered. Plan accordingly:
Keep a runbook for building a replacement cluster, and rehearse it once.
Keep the credentials for every source retrievable from your vault, because failover needs them.
Decide which sources are critical enough to keep a warm second cluster for.
Remember that VAs and clusters are per tenant, so production and sandbox each need their own.
Rolling updates need a pair. One appliance at a time is updated, so two keep the cluster up. SailPoint advises building a new cluster rather than moving existing appliances.

Build the network (firewall, DNS, NTP, proxy) before the image.
Change and vault the default password on first login.
Use one passphrase per cluster and store it.
Verify with Test Connection and a failover test before you attach production sources.

The cutover was uneventful because most of the risk had been moved earlier into a rollout plan, a staged attribute switch-on and a data reconciliation. This page describes that plan, the order of its steps, what does and does not migrate between tenants, and the data problems that had to be cleared before the HR feed could be trusted in production.

The plan was a spreadsheet of numbered tasks with an owner, a status and a dependency. Its phases, in order:
User acceptance testing. One cycle per application, with a sign-off. A pre-UAT check was done by someone other than the implementer.
Communications. An organisation-wide mail, an application-specific mail, an FAQ, a one-sheet and an enablement deck.
Change process. One change record per application through the change advisory board.
Pre go-live in production. Deploy the production tenant, create break-glass administrators, connect the virtual appliances, run a health scan, configure the HR source, identity profile and transforms, configure and validate single sign-on.
Migration of configuration. Transforms and rules, email templates, system configuration, branding, access profiles, roles and applications, governance groups and workflows, then the non-authoritative sources.
Aggregation and correlation analysis in production.

Cutover day. A production sanity test of one joiner and one leaver, a go or no-go decision, a rollback decision point and a soft go-live announcement.
Staged mover and attribute sync. See below.
Two things made this sequence work. Everything that could be verified without users (connectivity, data, correlation) was verified before communications went out, and the rollback decision was written down in advance, with an owner.

What to test, in order
Layer | Test | Evidence |
Connectivity | Each VA reaches each source; cluster status is healthy | VA health scan |
Aggregation | Account counts match the source; groups aggregated before accounts | Counts per source |
Correlation | Correlation rate per source; list of uncorrelated accounts reviewed | Uncorrelated report |
Lifecycle | One joiner, one mover, one leaver, one rehire per source | Test cases with before and after |
Provisioning | Create, enable, disable, group add and remove per connector, run for real | Source-side screenshot or query |
Requests | Each access profile requested, approved, fulfilled, revoked | Request IDs |
Forms and workflows | Every path, including denial and timeout | Execution log |
Notifications | Every template to the right recipient in each environment | Mail samples |
Test environment realities
Sandbox maps to the lower application environments, and production to production. JDBC URLs, database names, API endpoints and literals inside rules all differ. Keep an environment table and review it at promotion time.

Mail routing differs per environment. In sandbox, redirect all notifications to a test mailbox. In production, make sure the redirect is off. A notification matrix (template, trigger, recipient, environment) pays for itself.
Pre-UAT checks should not be done by the implementer. The implementer knows which cases to avoid.
Test with data that looks like production. Joiners with long names, apostrophes, double spaces, missing managers, rehires and employees on two contracts exposed more bugs than clean test data.
Evidence of a UAT sign-off
Record the application, the version of the design document, the test cases, the result of each, the issues and their disposition, and the name and date of the approver. We kept it per application so the approval was not a single "everything is fine" mail.

Config Hub was used to move configuration, and its limits shaped the plan.
Weekly automated backups and manual full backups were present and are cheap insurance. Take a manual full backup immediately before any cutover step.
A draft deploy was used to move forms.
Source secrets do not move. Expect to re-enter every credential in production. Make it a checklist item per source and treat it as the moment to issue production-specific credentials.
VAs and clusters are per tenant. They must be built and connected in production; they are not migrated.
Environment-specific values (connection strings, host names, database names, rule literals) must be changed after the deploy and before the first aggregation. Search exported rules for sandbox hostnames.
Order matters: transforms and rules first, then templates and system configuration, then access profiles, roles and applications, then governance groups and workflows, then sources that are not authoritative.
Promotion path. Take a manual full backup before any cutover step, preview an import first, and diff an export afterwards.

chunks.h: Data reconciliation before the HR feed goes live
chunks.x:
The first aggregation of production data is when historical neglect becomes visible. Findings before cutover:
More than 1,300 directory accounts had no employee id, so they could not be correlated. Treat that as a data clean-up to finish before the HR source is switched on, rather than a correlation rule that guesses.
The HR system carried years of historical leavers, which is why the tenant held about 43,000 identities for a workforce of about 13,000. Decide at design time how to treat them (exclude by population filter, or include as inactive). See the identity model page.
A data issues workbook and a production data analysis were kept as living artefacts, listing each issue, its owner and its status. Do not start cutover with items open and unowned.
Duplicate, double-space and case-differing names in the directory surfaced as account creation failures and correlation misses afterwards. Normalise or at least list them.

Before
This checklist combines what the rollout plan contained with what we would add; the plan itself listed break-glass administrators, VA connection and health scan, HR source configuration, single sign-on validation, the service-management mailbox and the approval groups.
Break-glass administrators exist, are tested and are documented.
VA health scan is green on every cluster.
HR source, identity profile and transforms are configured and validated against a sample.
Single sign-on is validated.
Notification templates are deployed and mail routing is set for production.
An IT service management mailbox and assignment group exist, and the integrator has queue access.
Governance groups and approval groups exist.
During
Aggregate the HR source and review counts.
Aggregate the directories and review correlation and uncorrelated lists.
Run the sanity test: one joiner, one leaver, end to end in production.

Go or no-go with named decision makers.
If go, announce a soft go-live.
If no-go, execute the rollback written into the plan. Our plan named the decision point and its owner; the mechanics (what to disable, what to restore from the pre-cutover backup) are yours to define and rehearse.
After
Nightly search exports of joiners and leavers for the first weeks, reviewed by the team. These were the earliest signal of data problems and were also the evidence base for hypercare.
Recommended, not observed: a daily check-in with the service desk and a change freeze except for fixes.

Switching on attribute sync from HR to the directory and applications was the highest-risk step because it writes to live accounts for thousands of people. We did it in stages:
The plan covered ten attributes only.
Location and country first, since location drives birthright access.
The remaining attributes in groups of at most two, over about ten days.
Validate between steps with a before and after sample.
Switch off on data issues and roll back the last step.
This is the cheapest rollback available. A staged switch-on turns a mass update into a series of small ones with a known last step.
Cheapest rollback. Location and country first, because location drives birthright access; the rest in groups of at most two.

Applications went live in waves, not on one day:
Directory and HR first.
Then the service management and client-facing tools.
Then the finance and investor systems.
The most sensitive client system last, about three weeks after the others.
The ordering rule was dependencies first, risk last. Each wave had its own change record, communication, UAT sign-off and rollback.

Org-wide mail ahead of cutover, application-specific mails per wave.
An FAQ and a one-sheet for managers, because managers carry the load of the new forms.
An enablement deck for the service desk.
A named mailbox for questions that is staffed.
Notifications deserve their own review. After go-live the team made seven changes to email notifications, all to fix who received what. See the hypercare page.

From the SaaS configuration reference and the Config Hub backup documentation, October 2026.
Config Hub facts
Backups. SailPoint backs up the production tenant weekly and keeps up to five. You can keep up to ten manual backups (delete one to add another), and a backup or draft holds up to 5,000 objects unless support raises it. Only manual backups can be deleted.
Secrets are never included. After a restore or deploy of sources, re-enter every secret and credential.
Restore means draft then deploy. You create a draft comparing a backup with the live tenant, optionally edit it, then deploy. Check the green dot that marks the live target before deploying, because the list can show several tenants.
Deploy does not delete. Objects that exist in the target but not in the draft stay.
Supported objects include access profiles, roles, access request configuration, attribute sync source configuration, campaign filters, connector rules and rules, form definitions, governance groups, identity profiles, lifecycle states, notification templates, password policies, segments, separation of duties policies, service desk integrations, sources, tags, transforms, trigger subscriptions and workflows. Import through the API is narrower than deploy: only sources, identity profiles, rules, connector rules, transforms, trigger subscriptions and identity object configuration can be imported.

Unsupported types are skipped silently. An import containing them still ends COMPLETE, with no warning naming what was skipped. Do not read COMPLETE as "everything moved". Use preview=true on the import to see reference and resolution errors first.
Non-employee sources cannot be imported or deployed. Deploying one creates a standard source in the target, which can cause trouble.
Cloud rules cannot be modified in migration, because they are signed. Connector rules need no review.
Objects that reference others by ID may not resolve in the target tenant. Edit the draft before deploying.
Replacing the HR system
If the HR platform changes around your go-live, follow SailPoint's sequence on the identity model page: move the HR system first, onboard the new source separately, create a mirrored identity profile, and migrate lifecycle state and other access-driving attributes last.
Readiness before the first working session

SailPoint asks for the network team at the connectivity kick-off and for the HR and directory owners. Have the VA count, placement and network method decided before the call. See the architecture page.

Write the rollout plan as numbered tasks with owners, dependencies and a rollback decision point.
Keep sandbox and production environment tables, and review them at every promotion.
Re-enter source credentials in production as new credentials.
Clear identity data problems (no employee id, duplicates, historical leavers) before the first production aggregation.
Switch on attribute sync in stages of one or two attributes, with validation and a rollback between steps.
Take a full backup before cutover, and run nightly joiner and leaver exports for the first weeks.
Go live in waves, dependencies first and the most sensitive system last.
