Actions
Everything ISC does to people starts with the authoritative source. On this program the HR system was the only real one, and the identity model built on it carried 60-odd attribute mappings, 40-odd transforms and a handful of cloud rules. Get this layer right and joiner, mover and leaver mostly behave. Get it wrong and every other page of this guide turns into firefighting.

chunks.h: Choose the authoritative source on purpose
chunks.x:
One authoritative source for the workforce. A second profile existed only for a few administrator identities loaded from a delimited file with no cluster. Keep secondary profiles tiny and give them a lower priority number than the main one so correlation stays predictable.
The HR system must carry what automation needs. If lifecycle automation needs a disable date, a time zone, a manager identifier or a reason for leaving, those fields must exist in HR and be mandatory. We added several integration-specific fields to the HR object: a disable-access date, an employment status flag for the identity system, a reason for leaving, the work location time zone, a last-modified timestamp, and fields to hold the email address and login name written back by ISC.
Mandatory means enforced. The design assumed the disable date and leave date were mandatory. Hypercare then produced cases where HR forgot to update the disable date, or entered the wrong last day, and the account stayed live or was cut early. Put validation in the HR system, not in a document.

chunks.h: Connecting a Salesforce-based HR system (Sage People)
chunks.x:
The HR system was Sage People, which runs on Salesforce. The ISC Web Services connector talked to its REST query API.
Aspect | What we did | Why it matters |
Authentication | OAuth token endpoint called by a custom authentication step; the token is mapped into the source and sent as a bearer header | Credentials for the token call end up in the endpoint body, so check how the source stores them (see the security page) |
Query | A SOQL query over the team member object joined to current employment, selecting around 40 fields | Select only what you map. Every extra field slows the sync and widens the blast radius of a rename |
Paging | Termination step reads the done flag and follows nextRecordsUrl until finished | Without correct pagination steps the connector reads one page and stops |
Schedule | Hourly, all 24 hours | Joiners and leavers react within an hour. The design promised hourly sync from day one |

chunks.h: Connecting a Salesforce-based HR system (Sage People)
chunks.x:
Timeout | 200 seconds | The first full load is large; size the timeout for it |
Delta | A delta query filtered on a last-modified field existed in the legacy design | Decide deliberately whether you use delta. Delta reads usually cannot detect records that disappeared, so even with delta you need periodic full aggregations |
Test connection | A query with a hard LIMIT 2 | Confirms the credential and endpoint only. It does not validate your projection |
Writeback to the HR system (email address, login name) used a PATCH to the same object. It is covered below.

The design pinned the whole lifecycle to one HR field: the unique employee identifier, stable for the whole journey of a person including leaving and rehire. Everything keys on it.
Concept | Rule |
Joiner | An identifier ISC has never seen, with status Active or Pre Joiner |
Mover | An identifier ISC already has, with any change in a mapped attribute |
Leaver | An existing identifier whose disable-access date is today or in the past, whatever the employment status says |
Rehire | An existing identifier returning to Active or Pre Joiner with an empty reason for leaving |
The rehire rule is an HR process, not an ISC feature
The platform cannot decide whether someone is a rehire or a new person. The program put a rule on HR:
Back within 6 months, same location and department: reuse the old identifier. ISC reactivates the old account.
Back within 6 months into a different department or location, or after 6 months in any case: HR creates a new record with a new identifier. ISC creates a new identity, a new login and a new mailbox.

The reason was data protection. In one case an ex-employee moved between countries and wanted to keep the old mailbox, which held another entity's client data. Reactivating the old account would have exposed it. The 6-month rule was written into the risk log as the mitigation and communicated to HR, and it still produced hypercare tickets from regions that had not got the message.

The profile mapped account attributes straight across (names, department, title, country code), referenced transforms for anything that needed cleaning, and called cloud rules for computed values.
Directory identifiers were also read back in from the target accounts (login name, mail, distinguished name of the user and the manager) so later steps could build on them.
Manager is correlated by comparing the manager's HR identifier to each identity's own identifier; for directory accounts the built-in manager correlation by account ID was used.
Transforms: use lookups, not nested conditionals
The legacy tool normalised location and country names with enormous nested IIF(Eq(...)) expressions: more than fifty location rewrites in a single expression, plus employee-type mappings. Replacing those with ISC lookup transforms was one of the best decisions of the build.
The transforms that were worth having:

Purpose | Examples |
Normalisation | Remove diacritical marks, trim, spaces collapse, lower and upper case |
Standards formats | E.164 phone, ISO 3166 country, RFC 5646 language, ISO 8601 date |
Lookups | Country name, location name, office location code, RDC maps, employee type |
Per-country contacts | HR contact, finance contact, local IT contact, driven by country or location lookups |
Directory builders | Active and disabled distinguished names, login name, mail nickname |
Date logic | Is the hire date today, past or future; is now past the end date |
Caveats:
Lookup tables hold business data inside the tenant. HR contacts, finance contacts and local IT contacts per country live in transform tables. They change monthly. Agree an owner, a delivery channel (we used a monthly file from HR) and a change procedure, or contacts go stale and mails go to people who left. Several hypercare tickets were exactly this.

Transforms reference transforms. A directory DN transform referenced a location lookup that referenced a trim. Test the chain with real values, including blanks.
A "default" on every lookup. A location missing from the table otherwise yields an empty value and, downstream, an account in the wrong container or none at all.
Keep a naming scheme. We had separate "on identity profile" and "SP" variants of several DN transforms. Pick one set and retire the rest, or you will edit the wrong one.

chunks.h: Cloud rules that compute identity attributes
chunks.x:
Cloud rules run inside ISC with no network access. The program used them for values that need real logic.
Rule | Computes | Notes |
Lifecycle state generator | The cloudLifecycleState attribute from HR status, end date and time zone | Several variants (temp, latest, extended) existed in the tenant. Only one is referenced by the profile; the rest are clutter and a trap |
Next processing date | The moment, in UTC, at which the identity's end date is reached at 22:00 local time | Used by schedule-driven leaver workflows |
Login name generator | The sAMAccountName | Described below |
Mail generator | The email address | Described below |
End-date eligibility | A flag for a SaaS payroll app's half-month disable schedule | Shows how business calendars end up in rules |
Things to know about cloud rules:
You cannot read them back through a normal GET. To see the code you export configuration (a single export call limited to the rule type), which creates an export job. Treat that as part of discovery.

chunks.h: Cloud rules that compute identity attributes
Cloud rules that compute identity attributes
chunks.x:
Design points that carry over:
A far-future default end date (year 9000) avoids null handling.
An invalid or missing time zone falls back to a sensible default rather than throwing.
Hour-level truncation makes the comparison deterministic for a rule that is recomputed on every refresh.
Leave statuses are not leavers. Paid and unpaid leave kept the identity active.
Log the inputs. The rule logs every input to every condition. That is verbose but it is the only way to explain a state change later.

chunks.h: Login names, emails and distinguished names
chunks.x:
Joiner automation generated three identifiers. The rules are small and every one of them produced hypercare tickets.
Identifier | Rule | Caveat |
Login name | First 3 letters of first name + last 3 letters of last name + a two-digit counter, 8 characters maximum | The counter increments until idn.accountExistsByDisplayName says it is free. We capped the loop at 2,000 attempts. Short names are padded with random letters |
Email | first.last, then first.last1, first.last2... on collision | Checked against the directory, not only ISC. Name changes generate a new address; the old one becomes a secondary alias |
Distinguished name | CN + region / department / work location path | The CN is the login name, so the directory's "Name" shows ABC123 rather than a human name |
That last point caused several tickets: after the cutover date, new users appeared in the directory console under their login name. The explanation that worked for service desks: the directory's Name attribute defaults to the CN, display name is a different attribute and is still the human name, Outlook and Teams use display name, and for audit reports you should export display name, CN, login name and Name together. Publish that note before go-live.

chunks.h: Login names, emails and distinguished names
chunks.x:
Display names
Double spaces. A name attribute built from a directory CN gave "First Last" for people without a middle name. Normalise with a collapse-spaces transform and search with that in mind.
Maiden names. If HR's full name includes a maiden name and you split it, you get "First Last Last". Build the display name from first name and last name only, and keep a separate attribute for the app that needs a different format.
Requested name changes. HR corrects a surname and expects a new email: that is a mover with a name change, handled by the directory before-provisioning logic (new address, UPN, SMTP and SIP proxy addresses, old SMTP kept as an alias). It needs to push the new address back to HR.

Email and login name must be written back to the HR system so downstream systems and HR users see them. The pattern that worked:
Event-driven workflow fires on a change of the email or login name attribute (ignoring the literal value none), waits briefly, then PATCHes the HR record.
Scheduled workflow runs twice a day and sweeps for identities whose values are not yet in HR, so a failed event is repaired automatically.
Both send a notification on failure.
Caveats from the program:
The HR OAuth call used a password grant, and the workflow HTTP step held the client secret in the body in plaintext. ISC lets you reference a stored secret in a workflow, but the secrets can only be created in the UI. Do that, not the plaintext version. See the workflows and security pages.
HR users kept asking "please push the work email into the HR system" for pre-joiners. The scheduled sweep exists because the event path is not perfect; tell HR the sweep interval so they know when to expect it.
Name corrections after the email was written back arrived as support requests ("push the new work email"). Decide who owns that path and whether it can be automated.

Account-to-identity correlation was attribute-based on almost every source. Conventions that emerged:
Source type | Typical sequence |
Directory | login name, then email |
Application with login = email | email only |
SQL applications | login name, then email, then employee number |
Mixed | email, then login name, then employee number |
Rules that follow from this:
Correlation is case sensitive unless you say otherwise. An email that differs only in case does not correlate, and the account lands in the uncorrelated pile rather than showing a mismatch. Set ignoreCase deliberately.
A single-attribute correlation with no fallback is fragile. An identity with no email cannot correlate at all.
Never correlate on a synthesised display name. One source built userName from first and last name in an after-rule; it was a display field, not a login.
Align correlation and provisioning. The attributes you correlate on should be the same ones the create policy writes, otherwise a freshly created account fails to correlate.
Plan for uncorrelated accounts. Access reviews need a source-owner campaign for them (see the campaigns page).

A pre-go-live reconciliation of directory accounts against HR found well over a thousand active directory accounts with no employee ID, plus a long tail of other mismatches (accounts for people HR no longer had, staff on unpaid leave, service-like accounts in human OUs). Do this analysis early:
Export directory accounts and HR records. Compare on employee ID, then email, then name.
Classify: matches, directory-only, HR-only, duplicates, non-human accounts in human OUs.
Agree a remediation owner and a deadline for each class. Backfilling the employee ID attribute in the directory is a legitimate one-off to enable correlation.
Define the standard human-account OU scope so the directory aggregation excludes service and shared accounts.

From the identity profile documentation, the account loading documentation and community threads on correlation and authoritative-source migration, checked October 2026.
Identity profiles
One identity belongs to one profile, the highest-priority profile where it has an account on that profile's authoritative source. Priority follows creation order (10, 20, and so on) and can be changed through the update-identity-profile API. Plan the order before you create overlapping profiles.
Required mappings: user name, work email and last name must be mapped in every profile and cannot be null. User name must be unique across identities; a duplicate raises an identity exception.
Do not use the characters * ( ) & ! . in the source attribute mapped to the user name or alternative sign-in attribute.
A multi-value attribute in a transform uses only its first value. Test with a person who has two.
You cannot create or delete an identity profile while an account aggregation is running.

Deleting a profile deletes its identities unless they can be reassigned, and their accounts become uncorrelated. Remove source-owner and app-owner links from those identities first, or the deletion fails.
After changing mappings the profile shows "Needs Processing". Apply the changes, and use Preview on the mappings page with real data first.
Rules need review by SailPoint before implementation; transforms do not. This is why a rule change can take calendar time.
Optimized aggregation and correlation
Why a fixed correlation rule can do nothing. Accounts that did not change are skipped, so they are never re-matched. Use the unoptimized run after correcting correlation logic or the data it matches.
This is the most useful addition to the correlation section above. By default an aggregation is optimized: it reads every record, but an existing account with no detected change is skipped and neither account correlation nor manager correlation is evaluated for it. Consequences:

Fixing a correlation rule, or fixing the data it matches on, does not re-correlate accounts that did not change. Accounts stay uncorrelated until you run an unoptimized aggregation.
Scheduled and manual runs from the UI are always optimized. An unoptimized run is available only through the API, by passing disableOptimization=true to the account-load call, and it applies to that run only.
Manually correlated accounts are kept on an unoptimized run, so check for them before you start.
Community practice for changing correlation: confirm the new attribute is populated, unique and immutable on every existing account, add it as the first criterion with the old one as a temporary fallback (criteria are evaluated in order), run the unoptimized aggregation, then review what is still uncorrelated. Community threads also report a default fallback that compares the account name with the identity name when no configured criterion matches, which can correlate an account you did not expect. Treat that as observed by others, not documented.

Priority matters for second sources. Plan the order before you create overlapping profiles; you cannot create or delete a profile while an account aggregation is running.
Choosing the join key
Both the documentation and the community's authoritative-source migration guide say the same thing we concluded: use an attribute that is unique, consistently captured in every system and immutable, and avoid personally identifiable values such as government identifiers.
Replacing or changing the HR system
SailPoint's migration guide gives a sequence worth adopting if the HR platform will change during or after your program:
Sequence from SailPoint's authoritative-source migration guide. Choose a low-impact window and keep a rollback plan with time to execute it.
Go live with the new HR system first and do not switch ISC to it the same day. Pause orchestrations and watch its data for a few days to a week.

Onboard the new HR source, let several aggregations run and configure manager correlation.
Correlate its accounts to existing identities on the agreed unique attribute and review the uncorrelated report.
Create a new identity profile mirroring the old mappings and transforms, confirm identity counts, then raise its priority.
Update role criteria with OR clauses so people qualify on either the old or new HR data.
Migrate attributes gradually with firstValid transforms, moving lifecycle state and other access-driving attributes last.
Re-point owners and governance groups, then delete the old profile.

Specify the HR fields automation needs and enforce them in HR.
Document the join key and the rehire rule and get HR's written agreement.
Replace conditional-heavy mappings with lookup transforms that have defaults, and name an owner for every table.
Keep one version of each cloud rule; export and archive the rest.
Publish the CN-equals-login-name explanation to service desks before go-live.
Reconcile directory accounts to HR at least a month before cutover.

chunks.h: Web Services and JDBC Connector Field Notes
chunks.x:
SailPoint ISC Greenfield Implementation Field Guide
On this page
Part 1: the Web Services connector
Part 2: the JDBC connector
Part 3: testing a custom integration
What SailPoint's documentation and community add
Actions
Web Services and JDBC are the two connectors that carry a custom integration. Both look configuration-driven and both are really code-driven: the interesting behaviour lives in connector rules. This page collects the mechanics, the traps and the patterns that worked.

Anatomy
A Web Services source is a list of endpoints, each tagged with an operation type: Test Connection, Custom Authentication, Account Aggregation, Group Aggregation, Get Object, Create, Update, Enable, Disable, Add Entitlement, Remove Entitlement. Some placeholders recur everywhere:
Placeholder or field | Meaning |
$application.<attr>$ | A connector attribute, for example the bearer token the authentication endpoint maintains |
$plan.<field>$ | A value from the provisioning plan |
$response.<field>$ | A field of the response in a chained Get Object call |
rootPath | JSONPath where the records start in the response |
resMappingObj | Maps response fields to schema attributes. An attribute absent from it is never populated, even if the schema declares it and the API returns it |
parentEndpointName | Chains a Get Object call to an aggregation call, so a list returns thin records and each is fetched in full. Aggregation becomes N+1 |

beforeRule / afterRule | Attach a connector rule to an endpoint |
possibleHttpErrors, authenticationFailedErrorMsg | Let the connector recognise an application-level error inside an HTTP 200 |
encrypted | The list of connector attributes stored encrypted. Anything not on it can be returned in clear text by the API |
throwProvBeforeRuleException, throwProvAfterRuleException | When true, an exception in a rule fails the operation instead of being swallowed. Leave both true |
Rule hook points. Rules run on the appliance, around the connector's own call. Logic that looks missing from the endpoint configuration is usually in the before rule.
Authentication
Use a Custom Authentication endpoint when the API issues its own tokens: ISC posts the credentials, reads the token from the response, and stores it in an encrypted attribute that every other endpoint references.
Traps seen:
Expired tokens returned as HTTP 200. One application returned 200 with TOKEN_EXPIRED or JWT token expired! in the body, not 401. The connector only re-authenticates if those strings are listed in authenticationFailedErrorMsg and possibleHttpErrors. Misspell one or let the vendor reword it and error bodies flow into the account pipeline as data, with no alert.

Tokens with no refresh. A 24-hour maximum token with no refresh token means the connector re-authenticates from scratch. Fine, but it makes the token endpoint a single point of failure.
The token endpoint can fail under concurrency. In a sandbox test, five simultaneous request submissions timed out 5 out of 5 on one vendor's token endpoint. Stagger bulk work.
Rules that mint their own tokens. Two rules on one source requested a token with the service account name and password embedded as query parameters in a URL literal in the rule source. When the service credential rotates it must be changed in the source and each rule, and a live GET of the rule returns the credential in clear text. Use $application.token$ or a connector attribute instead.
Credential halves left in clear. An API client id and secret pair was split: the secret was on the encrypted list, the id was not. Add every credential-like attribute to encrypted and then verify through the API that it returns masked.

Pagination, volume and ceilings
Pattern | What happens |
Single page with a large pageSize, enableHasMore false, no paging steps | Works until the population exceeds the page size. Then the overflow is silently dropped. On a later run those accounts look deleted and, if the delete threshold allows, are removed with their entitlement links |
Real pagination with paginationSteps | Follow a "next page" indicator; a Salesforce-style done flag plus nextRecordsUrl was used for HR |
N+1 Get Object | A 600-account population needs about 600 sequential calls. Raise the timeout (180 s versus a 120 s norm) and pick a quiet window |
No partitioning, no delta | Every run is a full sweep. Partitioning is the lever if the population grows |
An API built for the integration | May return everything in one response; no pagination needed. Confirm with the owner, do not assume |
Add population monitors: record the number of accounts returned per run and alert on a sudden drop or a count that sits exactly at a page size.

Made a second HTTP call to merge in data the first call cannot return, for example a disabled-users list, or the second half of a group catalogue.
Synthesised a display name from first and last name.
Cautions:
Caution | Detail |
Allowlist beats denylist | Copy named fields onto a fresh map. Stripping a denylist lets any new vendor field flow into the account. The allowlist has the opposite cost: a new field is dropped until the rule changes. Pick on purpose |
Set both flag directions | A rule that only sets IIQDisabled: true depends on absence meaning enabled |
Exact-string status checks | "InActive".equals(status) stops matching on Inactive, INACTIVE, 0 or a JSON boolean. Normalise first |
Fail loudly on a second call | If the second call cannot be made (no token), log an unmistakable line and alert on it. Otherwise the population looks entirely enabled |
Logging level | One rule logged every account at error level on every run, with the whole list, daily. Wrong severity buries real errors |

Debug flags | Keep a LOGGING_ENABLED-style flag, default false, and switch it on only for a diagnostic window |
Unreachable code | Dead statements after a return hide mistakes. Delete them |
Before-rules: rewriting what gets sent
A before-rule receives the endpoint and the provisioning plan and returns a modified endpoint. They are used when the plan placeholders cannot build the request.
The endpoint body can be dead configuration. If the rule replaces the body, anything written in the endpoint's body field is misleading. We found endpoints whose jsonBody was null, and others whose body used a different key than the rule sent. Document that "the rule is the only place the request exists".
One rule for both add and remove. A single rule can serve both entitlement directions by reading each attribute request's own operation. Editing it changes both directions at once.
Substitution-string encodings. One product took parameters as a flat string of comma-separated name=value pairs, with square brackets around values containing spaces. The rule builds the string. A value containing a comma or a bracket breaks it, and nothing escapes it.

Swallowed exceptions. Wrapping the whole loop in try/catch (Exception) { log } converts a loud failure into a request with blank substitution variables. Let the exception propagate so the operation fails.
Only some attributes sync. A before-rule that builds an update body from a switch over attribute names only supports the names in the switch. Anything else produces a plan that reaches the target with the field absent and succeeds. Name this limit in your capability statement.
Policy-only fields. A field can exist only in the provisioning policy so the rule can read it, never in the schema. It will never appear on an aggregated account. That is elegant and looks like a mistake if you do not know it.
Environment values hard-coded in rules. Base URL, application name and API version appeared as literals in both the endpoint and the rules. A URL change is a rule change. Read them from connector attributes.

HTTP library choice. HttpURLConnection cannot send PATCH (use GET then PUT instead). An Apache HTTP client inside a rule produced consecutive aggregation errors and was reverted. Use the connector's own WebServicesClient.
Time-limited calls. A call that exceeds the VA timeout (63 seconds in our measurement) wedged that requester for about an hour: every later request from the same identity came back cancelled.
Revocation done in rules
On one REST integration the Remove Entitlement endpoint did almost nothing. Two before-rules, about 400 lines each, read live grants from the target, decided between removing one role, deleting a grant row or disabling the user, and called four endpoints directly.
Read the rules, not the endpoint, to learn what revocation does. A benefit of this design: it reads live data, so revocation stays correct even when the aggregated view in ISC is months old.
The debug webhook

Four production rules across the tenant posted diagnostics to an internal HTTP listener through a sendLog helper. Two versions existed:
Version | When the listener is down |
Unsafe: throws a runtime exception, no timeouts | The operation fails or hangs |
Safe: catches, logs a warning, 2-second timeouts | The operation continues |
Remove debug webhooks before production. If you must keep one, use the safe version and a flag set to false.
Names with whitespace
Two traps cost real time:
A schema named with two spaces between words propagates into every endpoint operation type and connector attribute. A single-space search finds nothing. Renaming detaches every entitlement and access profile, so leave it.
Two rules in the same set carried a double space after a prefix; the other two did not. Looking up by the "obvious" name returned nothing.
Header values with trailing spaces or leading spaces in keys are harmless until a stricter server arrives.

Choose names without whitespace in the first place and lint for it.
Test Connection is not a test
Test Connection often calls a trivial endpoint (LIMIT 2, a filter that matches nothing). It proves reachability and authentication, not the aggregation projection. After a change, run a small-scope aggregation and compare counts and status distribution.

Anatomy
Attribute | Purpose |
SQL / <schema>.SQL | The aggregation query for a schema |
getObjectSQL | Single-account read, with the native identity substituted |
testConnSQL | Used by Test Connection |
url, user, password, driverClass | The connection |
buildMapRule | A JDBCBuildMap rule that runs per result-set row |
jdbcProvisionRule | A JDBCProvision rule that does all writes |
There is no provisioning SQL on the source. createSQL, updateSQL, enableSQL and the entitlement maps are all null. Every write is a PreparedStatement opened inside the provisioning rule. To know what provisioning does, read the rule.
Configuration traps
Three copies of every setting. The UI writes the account schema's settings under the bare name, an undefined. prefix and, for groups, both Group. and group.. They are normally identical. On one source they were not: two different host addresses for the same database. Which was used depended on how the schema was addressed. Edit through the UI so all copies stay in step, and check all prefixes after any API change.

The driver JAR is per source. A driver upgrade is repeated on every JDBC source.
Duplicate entries in the encrypted list (privateKey, passphrase twice, an undefined.password) suggest hand editing. Tidy, but verify each name against a real attribute first.
Environment names hard-coded in rule SQL. A sandbox rule backup named the sandbox database in every statement, so promoting it unchanged would point production at the sandbox. Parameterise environment-specific names.
A production source on an instance named like a test instance. Confirm instance names with the DBA team.
Aggregation SQL traps
Trap | Effect |
TOP (1000) | Silently truncates a catalogue |
Hard-coded ID lists for groups (WHERE ID = 254 OR ID = 255) | Adding a group means editing SQL; there is no category filter |
Filter IsWindowADAccount = '1' | Only AD-linked accounts are visible. Counts are not user counts. A user who stops being AD-linked drops out and is deleted next run |

Join to a group-user table producing a row per user-group pair | With isMulti: false and mergeRows: false, ISC has no instruction to merge rows into one account with two entitlement values. Set the attribute multi-valued and enable row merging |
Status baked into the entitlement value | Same group-client pair exists as active and inactive values, inflating counts and campaigns |
Schema with identity and display inverted | An access form drawing options from the schema empties if you change the identity attribute |
Build-map rules
A build-map rule turns one row into an account map. A brittle version:
java
```
Map map = JDBCConnector.buildMapFromResultSet(result, schema);
Boolean status = (Boolean) map.get("IsActive");   // throws on null or a non-boolean
if (status == false) map.put("IIQDisabled", true);
return map;
```
If the column is null or the driver returns a different type, the cast throws and that row fails. The account silently drops out of the aggregation and later becomes a deletion candidate. A robust version:

java
```
Map map = JDBCConnector.buildMapFromResultSet(result, schema);
Object v = map.get("IsActive");
boolean active = v != null && "true".equalsIgnoreCase(String.valueOf(v));
map.put("IIQDisabled", !active);
return map;
```
Provisioning rules
Patterns that worked:
Dispatch on AccountRequest.Operation: Create, Modify, Disable, Enable, Delete.
Use a transaction for multi-table writes. The most robust rule inserted into three tables with auto-commit off, committed on success, and rolled back on a SQL exception, then set STATUS_FAILED.
Check for duplicates before inserting an assignment.
Resolve names to IDs inside the rule (role name to role ID) rather than expecting ISC to supply IDs.
Refuse delete explicitly with a clear message; accounts are disabled, not deleted.
Call a stored procedure when the target has complex side effects. Let the application team own the procedure and its tests.
Treat the status flags as two-sided. Disabling set one status column in one table and another account-status column in a second table, and enabling reversed both and cleared the termination date.

Gotchas:
Gotcha | Detail |
An undeclared variable gates the whole create path | A rule's guard condition referenced two identifiers that were never declared (a corrupted spelling and a case mismatch). The condition could never evaluate as intended. The modify path, used by most requests, had separate code and worked, so nobody noticed. Exercise every operation in a lower environment, especially create for a person with no existing account |
Failures in the target but not the mirror | See below |
Credentials in rules | Rules on the Web Services sources carried service credentials as URL query parameters; check JDBC rules for embedded connection strings too. Rotation must change the source and every rule |
Rule gate uses the access request comments | See below |
Carrying extra provisioning data: the comments channel
The ISC provisioning plan has no field for "which database" or "which client". Two integrations needed to insert several entitlement values in one write (role plus office plus client; group plus client plus database). The solution:

Grant the entitlement any other way (API call, role, certification remediation, access profile) | No comments arrive; the rule throws and provisioning fails |
The only supported way to grant that entitlement is the launcher. Say so on the page where someone might try another route, or make the rule fall back to deriving the values from the entitlement itself. Change the workflow and the rule as one unit.
A central database in front of many databases
One application used a database per client. ISC cannot aggregate across many databases through one source. The solution was a centralised mirror schema that holds users, entitlements and a client-to-database map, with a stored procedure that writes into the right client database.
Consequences to design for:
Every provisioning operation writes twice: through the procedure into the real client database, and into the mirror so the next aggregation sees it.

If the procedure fails but the mirror write succeeds, ISC reports the mirror's view and re-provisioning looks like a no-op. "ISC says I have it, the application says no" is the symptom.
The client-to-database map is itself an entitlement. A change to the schema's identity attribute empties the client dropdown on the request form.
A dedicated-instance sibling of the same application used plain SQL per client with a fixed group list; a shared, hard-coded build map served both.
Secrets, rotation and rule inventory
41 connector rules existed. Maintain an inventory: rule name, type, the source it is attached to, and every place it hard-codes an environment value or credential.
A rule is a record you can read with a normal API call. Exports and shared copies should be scrubbed of connection strings, query-string credentials and long hex literals.
Unattached rules (templates, older versions) accumulate. Prune them or label them.

A checklist that would have caught most of the defects above:
Test Connection, then a small-scope aggregation, then a full one. Compare account and entitlement counts to the target.
Status: confirm a known-disabled account aggregates as disabled and a known-enabled one as enabled. Change a wording in the target in a lower environment and confirm the failure is visible.
Overflow: temporarily reduce a page size or TOP and confirm you can see the drop.
Run each provisioning operation in a lower environment: create (for a person who has no account), enable, disable, add each entitlement type, remove each type, and an unsupported operation.
Run the same operation by every legitimate route (form, access profile, role, API).
Simulate a target outage mid-operation and confirm the plan fails rather than reports success.
Look in the target and confirm the result. Do not trust the ISC status.
Re-aggregate and confirm ISC shows the change.

Rotate the credential and confirm where it must change.
Turn logging on, read the log of one run, and turn it off.

chunks.h: What SailPoint's documentation and community add
chunks.x:
API rate limits
The rate limit documentation states a default of 100 requests per client ID and API version per 10 seconds. Exceeding it returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header giving the seconds to wait. Individual APIs may differ, so check each specification. Practical impact for this guide:
A script that loops over campaigns, sources or profiles needs backoff. Plan concurrency around the client ID, not the token, and note that two scripts sharing one client share the allowance.
Do not give every tool the same administrator client. Separate clients give separate allowances and a usable audit trail.
The Web Services connector backs off on 429 using Retry-After. Community reports describe a limited number of retries, so a vendor API with a tight limit can still fail an aggregation. Check the vendor's own limit before choosing page size and concurrency.
Provisioning retries

chunks.h: What SailPoint's documentation and community add
chunks.x:
Community threads describe a retry mechanism for provisioning: a retryable error is retried a limited number of times (three is commonly quoted), configured per source through retryableErrors with optional provisioningMaxRetries and provisioningRetryThreshold. Reports conflict on whether the threshold can be tuned and whether the spacing is one minute or one hour, and one report quotes support saying the values are fixed. Treat retries as a behaviour to test on your tenant, not a setting to rely on. Match error codes or stable message fragments, not messages containing dates or sequence numbers.
Pagination cautions from the community
Identify the application's real paging parameter first; many are not startIndex.
Offset paging can break when data changes during the run. If the vendor offers a cursor or query token, prefer it.
Large page sizes can time out. One thread reports aggregation timing out above a count of 200.

chunks.h: What SailPoint's documentation and community add
chunks.x:
A TERMINATE_IF check on record count must be placed correctly relative to the offset increment, or the loop ends early.
Mixing connectors is legitimate. A JDBC source for aggregation with a web-services path for provisioning is a documented community pattern where the application has no aggregation API.

Reusable fragments for the parts of an ISC build that are not rules: workflow expressions and step patterns, the search queries that drive cascading forms, and the API calls an engineer reaches for. Names in angle brackets are placeholders. API paths and versions change, so confirm them against the current reference. Nothing here should be run against production before you have run it in sandbox.

A token
bash
```
TENANT=<tenant>
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST "https://$TENANT.api.identitynow.com/oauth/token" \
  -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \
  -d "client_id=$CLIENT_ID" \
  -d "client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET" | jq -r .access_token)
```
Read the client id and secret from your vault or the environment, never from the script. A token is short-lived, so fetch one per run. If you loop over many objects, pace the calls: the default allowance is 100 requests per client and API version per 10 seconds, and a 429 carries a Retry-After header.
bash
```
api() {   # api GET /v2025/sources
  local m=$1 p=$2; shift 2
  while :; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /tmp/resp.json -w '%{http_code}' -X "$m" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      "https://$TENANT.api.identitynow.com$p" "$@")
    if [ "$code" = "429" ]; then sleep 5; continue; fi
    cat /tmp/resp.json; return $([ "$code" -lt 400 ])
  done
}
```

Read-only calls you will use every week
bash
```
api GET "/v2025/sources?limit=250&offset=0"
api GET "/v2025/sources/<id>"
api GET "/beta/sources/<id>/schedules"
api GET "/v2025/entitlements?filters=source.id eq \"<id>\"&limit=250"
api GET "/v2025/access-profiles?limit=250"
api GET "/beta/source-apps/<id>/access-profiles?limit=250"
api GET "/v2025/workflows"
api GET "/v2025/form-definitions"
```
Always page at 250 or below. The source-app sub-resource returns an empty list if limit exceeds 250.
Search
The search API is the verification and monitoring tool. A request names the index and a query:
json
```
POST /v2025/search
{
  "indices": ["accounts"],
  "query": { "query": "source.name:\"<source name>\" AND disabled:true" },
  "sort": ["id"],
  "limit": 250
}
```
Counts only, for a monitor:
json
```
POST /v2025/search?count=true
{ "indices": ["accounts"], "query": { "query": "source.name:\"<source name>\" AND uncorrelated:true" }, "limit": 1 }
```

Page through a large result by sorting on a stable field and passing the last value of the previous page as searchAfter.
Question | Index | Query idea |
Disabled accounts on a source | accounts | source.name:"X" AND disabled:true |
Uncorrelated accounts | accounts | source.name:"X" AND uncorrelated:true |
Directly requestable entitlements | entitlements | requestable:true, compared with your intended list |
Who joined or left | identities | a created-date or lifecycle-state query |
Entitlements for a cascade step | entitlements | see below |
Field names vary by index and release. Check them with a one-row query before you build a monitor on them.
Force a full re-correlation of one source
An optimized aggregation skips unchanged accounts, so fixed correlation logic is not re-run. The API can disable optimization for one run:
bash
```
curl -X POST "https://$TENANT.api.identitynow.com/v3/sources/<id>/load-accounts" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "disableOptimization=true"
```

It reprocesses every record, keeps manually correlated accounts, and applies to that run only. Check the delete threshold before you run it.
Patching a source
Sources are changed with a JSON patch:
text
```
PATCH /v3/sources/<id>      Content-Type: application/json-patch+json
```
json
```
[
  { "op": "replace", "path": "/connectorAttributes/deleteThresholdPercentage", "value": 10 },
  { "op": "add",     "path": "/connectorAttributes/mergeRows", "value": true }
]
```
Take a copy of the source (GET /v2025/sources/<id>) before every patch, and store it. Secrets are not returned, and some updates replace a whole attribute, so check the result by reading it back.
Export cloud rules and configuration
Cloud rules cannot be read with a GET. Use the configuration export:
json
```
POST /beta/sp-config/export
{ "description": "rule export", "includeTypes": ["RULE"], "objectOptions": {} }
```
Then poll the export job and download it. The export needs an administrator and creates a job, not a change. Treat the result as sensitive: rules can contain credentials.

Expressions seen in the program's workflows:
Expression | Meaning |
$.trigger.launchedBy.id | The person who launched an interactive workflow |
$.interactiveForm.formData.<field> | An answer from the first form. The key is the form element, with its exact capitalisation |
$.interactiveForm4.formData.<field> | An answer from a later form in the same workflow (numbered by step) |
$.loop.loopInput | The current item inside a loop |
$.loop.context.<step>... | A value from outside the loop, read from inside it |
{{...}} | A template placeholder. If it cannot be resolved it renders as literal text, so a typo corrupts a payload silently |
.JSON() | The only stringify function. Others render literally |
Step actions used
Action | Used for |
Interactive form | Ask the requester. The answers return inline |
sp:access:get | Find an access item by search. Returns id, name and type, not the value |
sp:access:manage | Grant or revoke an access item for an identity, with comments |

sp:http (version 3) | Call an API, including search, returning the raw response |
sp:manage-account | Enable or disable an existing account |
sp:forms | Raise an approval form and wait for the result |
Wait | Separate dependent provisioning events |
Send email | Notify the requester and the requestee |
Loop | Iterate a multi-select. The parallel loop accepts at most 250 items |
A cascade, step by step
This is the multi-step form pattern described in the complex applications page.
# | Step | Configuration |
1 | Interactive form | Scope, requestee, role selection |
2 | Get identities | The requestee from the form, the requester from the trigger |
3 | Compare | Branch on the scope value |
4 | HTTP search | Search entitlements for the next list (see below) |
5 | Interactive form | Populate a dropdown from the search result and let the user choose |
6 | Loop over the choices | For each: resolve the role, resolve the entity, grant the role |

7 | Wait | One minute between the role and the entity grant |
8 | Grant the entity | With comments linking it to the role |
9 | Email | Requester and requestee |
Search queries behind the dropdowns
text
```
# the entities for a chosen country
description.exact:"<country>" AND source.name.exact:"<source>" AND attribute.exact:"<entity attribute>"

# the entities for a chosen country and client, where the client is stored as a tag
description.exact:"<country>" AND source.name.exact:"<source>" AND attribute.exact:"<client entity attribute>" AND tags:"<normalised client>"

# one exact access item, by name and source
name.exact:"<role name>" AND source.name.exact:"<source>"
```
Rules for building them:
Quote string values and keep .exact where you need an exact match.
Store whatever the search must filter on in description, attribute or tags. Entitlement attributes are not indexed.
A list passed into the query renders like [5 2] and fails. Build tags:("A" "B") as an explicit OR from strings.

Normalise client names once (remove &, -, spaces, brackets and full stops) and use the same rule when you create the tags.
The comment that carries data to a rule
Set it on the grant step, and read it in the provisioning rule:
text
```
RoleId:<role>, EntityID:<entity>, Source:<source>
```
json
```
{"RequestedGroup":"<group>","RequestedClientName":"<client>","TargetDatabase":"<db>"}
```
Keep one format per source. A grant by any other route carries no comment, and the rule should refuse it with a clear message.
Calling the account-create API from a workflow
text
```
POST /v2025/accounts
```
This runs the connector's create operation and its before rules. It is the way to create an account on demand from a workflow, since there is no create-account action. Link to the identity is by correlation, not in the call.
json
```
{
  "attributes": {
    "sourceId": "<source id>",
    "<attribute>": "<value>"
  }
}
```

(Confirm the body for your release.) Use a test identity first.
Secrets in workflows
Secrets can only be created in the UI. A literal secret written through the API is dropped silently.
A full PUT of a workflow wipes a UI-set secret. Read the workflow first and preserve the reference.
One OAuth reference per workflow: avoid two steps with different credentials in one workflow.
Never put a client secret in an HTTP body.

Need | Use |
Show a field only after another is filled | A condition on the parent element, empty or not-empty |
Show a section | SHOW works on a section, not on an element |
Text the user must see | The field label. Section labels are not rendered |
Operators | EQ, CO, NOT_CO, IN, NOT_IN, SW, EW, on strings and booleans |
A second dependent list | A second form, fed by the workflow |
Retire a form | Never delete it while a launch may still point at it |

Build these as scheduled searches or as scripted checks, one per source:
Monitor | Query | Alert when |
Population | Count of accounts on the source | Drops sharply, or sits exactly on a page size |
Disabled count | Accounts with disabled:true | Moves by more than a small percentage between runs |
Uncorrelated | Accounts with uncorrelated:true | Grows |
Freshness | The last aggregation date per source | Older than the schedule plus a margin |
Entitlement count | Entitlements per source | Halves between runs |
Failed workflow executions | The workflow executions API, by status | The rate rises |

Keep the cascade queries and the normalisation rule in the integration notes.
Test the comment format with the grant routes you do not expect, so you know how the rule fails.
Treat every exported rule or workflow as sensitive.
